General Quantification of Covariate and Concept Shifts

Hongbo Chen Affiliation: Department of Statistics and Financial Mathematics, School of Mathematics, South China University of Technology, Guangzhou, China. First author: Hongbo Chen <hongboc616@gmail.com>    Li Charlie Xia Affiliation: Department of Statistics and Financial Mathematics, School of Mathematics, South China University of Technology, Guangzhou, China. First author: Hongbo Chen <hongboc616@gmail.com> Correspondence to: lcxia@scut.edu.cn
Abstract

Generalization under distribution shift remains a core challenge in modern machine learning, yet existing learning bound theory is limited to narrow, idealized settings and is non-estimable from samples. In this paper, we bridge the gap between theory and practical applications. We first show that existing definition of concept shift breaks when the source and target supports mismatch. Leveraging entropic optimal transport, we propose a key notion: γ∗\gamma^{*}\!-concept shifts, and derive a general error bound unifying covariate and γ∗\gamma^{*}\!-concept shifts, which applies to broad loss functions, label spaces, and stochastic labeling. We further develop estimators for these shifts with concentration guarantees, and the DataShifts algorithm, which can quantify distribution shifts and estimate the error bound in most applications - a rigorous and general tool for analyzing learning error under distribution shift.

Keywords: 
Machine Learning, ICML

1 Introduction

With the growth of data and computing power, supervised learning has achieved remarkable success. Nonetheless, traditional supervised learning assumes that the training data (source domain) and the test or deployment data (target domain) share the same distribution. However, in many real-world applications, the test data distribution can differ substantially from the training distribution, and this discrepancy can significantly impact model performance in the target domain. To analyze such challenges, researchers theorized that the distributions between the source and target domains are shifted and developed methods to assess how learners trained in the source domain could perform on the target domain. Depending on whether the target domain data is accessible, the problems are further categorized into domain adaptation and domain generalization.

Theoretical results on distribution shift usually bound a model’s target domain error by its source domain error plus a measure of the distribution shift. The shift is further dissected into X (covariate) and Y∣\midX (concept) shifts (Moreno-Torres et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2023). Early studies proposed using ℋ\mathcal{H}-divergence to measure X shift and derived an error bound for binary classification (Ben-David et al., 2006; Ben-David et al., 2010). Later works improved X shift using the maximum mean discrepancy (Long et al., 2015) and the Wasserstein distance (Shen et al., 2018; Courty et al., 2017). Further studies proposed more complex metrics for the X shift to obtain bounds for multiclass classification (Zhang et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2019). These results focused only on X shift and additionally relied on a joint-error term between the source and target domains. Lately, Zhao et al. (2019) improved this loose joint-error term and proposed a bound that explicitly considers both X and Y∣\midX shifts for binary classification, and Zhang et al. (2023) extended the theory to multiclass classification.

In this paper, we focus on two remaining key problems in the existing theoretical frameworks, which significantly hinder researchers from analyzing X and Y∣\midX shifts in applications:

  • •

    Generalizability. Existing theories rely on restrictive assumptions: they require deterministic labeling, omitting label noise and latent confounders commonly seen in practice; moreover, they only apply to classification with absolute error, excluding broader tasks such as regression and loss families.

  • •

    Estimability. Although existing theories provide a preliminary definition of Y∣\midX shift, this definition and the accompanying error bounds—are not estimable. As a result, one cannot rigorously quantify Y∣\midX shift on real data, nor assess its impact on model performance.

We aim to provide a general theoretical framework unifying X and Y∣\midX shifts that widely applies to stochastic labeling, most supervised tasks, and broader loss functions. Moreover, these two shifts can be accurately estimated from samples, thereby offering a rigorous, plug-and-play tool for quantifying and analyzing distribution shifts in real applications.

Specifically, our key observation is that if X shift occurs, the supports of the source and target covariate distributions may not overlap. Such a support mismatch renders the existing theories’ Y∣\midX shift ill-defined, fundamentally causing the error bounds non-estimable and loose. Our key innovation is to employ the entropic optimal transport to give a general definition for X and Y∣\midX shift. The γ∗\gamma^{*}-Y∣\midX shift we propose, which depends on the entropic optimal transport coupling of X shift, stays well-defined even when supports mismatch, and applies to the stochastic labeling and general label space. Based on that, we derived a new error bound that considers both the X and the γ∗\gamma^{*}-Y∣\midX shifts. Our new bound relies only on the Lipschitz continuity of the hypothesis hh and loss ℓ\ell, and is agnostic to specific hypothesis space, label space, or loss function, which naturally generalizes to binary and multiclass classification, regression and other tasks.

Since our γ∗\gamma^{*}-Y∣\midX shift is well-defined regardless of support mismatch, X and Y∣\midX shifts, and our new error bound becomes estimable from samples. Nonetheless, for X shift, the traditional plug-in estimator for entropic optimal transport tends to overestimate due to the curse of dimensionality. We thus further developed a debiased estimator that remains accurate in high dimensions. For our γ∗\gamma^{*}-Y∣\midX shift, we also proposed an estimator. We proved both estimators’ concentration inequalities to their true values. Leveraging these two estimators, we presented the DataShifts algorithm, enabling quantification of X and Y∣\midX shifts on general labeled data. Finally, we apply our theoretical framework and DataShifts to three distinct tasks: Novozymes enzyme prediction, ColoredMNIST, and PACS, clearly validating the general effectiveness of our theoretical results.

Contributions. In summary, our major contributions are:

  • •

    We show that support mismatch makes the existing Y∣\midX shift ill-defined—hence loose and non-estimable. We introduce the γ∗\gamma^{*}-Y∣\midX shift as a well-defined concept shift, which possesses many desirable properties.

  • •

    We derive a general error bound unifying covariate and γ∗\gamma^{*}\!-concept shifts. Our bound covers broader learning scenarios, far beyond traditional binary classification.

  • •

    For the X and γ∗\gamma^{*}-Y∣\midX shifts in our theory, we propose two estimators and prove their concentration inequalities, ensuring that these shifts can be rigorously estimated from finite samples.

  • •

    We integrate our theoretical results into the DataShifts algorithm, which can estimate X and γ∗\gamma^{*}-Y∣\midX shifts from real data, supplying a rigorous and general tool for quantifying and analyzing distribution shifts.

The paper is organized as follows: Section 2 covers the preliminaries, Section 3 presents the population-level theoretical results, Section 4 focuses on the statistical results, and Section 5 presents experiments validating our theory.

2 Preliminary

2.1 Problem Setup

Our problem is to bound the error of models under distribution shift. Let 𝒳\mathcal{X} and 𝒴\mathcal{Y} be the covariate space and the label space, respectively. Let 𝒟X​YS\mathcal{D}_{XY}^{S} and 𝒟X​YT\mathcal{D}_{XY}^{T} be the joint distributions of covariates and labels on 𝒳×𝒴\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y} for the source and target domains, respectively. 𝒟XS\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S}, 𝒟XT\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T} are their covariate marginals on 𝒳\mathcal{X}. For any x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}, we let 𝒟Y|X=xS\mathcal{D}_{Y|X=x}^{S} and 𝒟Y|X=xT\mathcal{D}_{Y|X=x}^{T} be the conditional label distributions at xx in the source and target domain. Let 𝒴′\mathcal{Y}^{\prime} be the output space of the learner, ℓ:𝒴×𝒴′→ℝ\ell:\mathcal{Y}\times\mathcal{Y}^{\prime}\to\mathbb{R} the loss, and ℋ⊆{g:𝒳→𝒴′}\mathcal{H}\subseteq\{g:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}^{\prime}\} the hypothesis space. For a hypothesis h∈ℋh\in\mathcal{H}, the learning errors for source and target domains are:

ϵS​(h)=𝔼(xS,yS)∼𝒟X​YS​[ℓ⁡(yS,h⁡(xS))]\epsilon_{S}(h)=\mathbb{E}_{(x_{S},y_{S})\sim\mathcal{D}_{XY}^{S}}\bigl[\ell(y_{S},h(x_{S}))\bigr]\\
ϵT​(h)=𝔼(xT,yT)∼𝒟X​YT​[ℓ⁡(yT,h⁡(xT))]\epsilon_{T}(h)=\mathbb{E}_{(x_{T},y_{T})\sim\mathcal{D}_{XY}^{T}}\bigl[\ell(y_{T},h(x_{T}))\bigr]

We hope to bound ϵT​(h)\epsilon_{T}(h) by ϵS​(h)\epsilon_{S}(h) and a measure of distribution shift, consistent with existing theoretical results (Ben-David et al., 2006; Zhao et al., 2019). Notably, the space 𝒳\mathcal{X} can be the raw input space or a representation space output by an upstream learner (Ben-David et al., 2006). Our theory treats them in the same way, so it applies to both raw data and learned representations.

Stochastic and deterministic labeling.

Above, we assume that the label yy follows the conditional distribution at point xx: y∼𝒟Y|X=xy\sim\mathcal{D}_{Y|X=x}, namely the stochastic labeling setting (Zhao et al., 2019). It enables our theory to accommodate latent confounders and label noise, which are common in practice. In contrast, existing theories oversimplify by using deterministic labeling: a labeling function f:𝒳→𝒴f:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y} with y=f⁡(x)y=f(x), a special case of stochastic labeling in which the conditional distribution collapses to a Dirac mass at f⁡(x)f(x), i.e., 𝒟Y|X=x=δf⁡(x)\mathcal{D}_{Y|X=x}=\delta_{f(x)}.

2.2 Existing Theory and Ill-Defined Y∣\midX Shift

We first demonstrate that support mismatch leads to an ill-defined Y∣\midX shift, a key flaw in existing theory.

Definition 2.1 (Support).

Let μ\mu be a probability measure on the topological space (𝒳,τ)(\mathcal{X},\tau). Its support is defined as:

supp(μ)={x∈𝒳∣∀U∈τ,x∈U,μ(U)>0}\operatorname{supp}(\mu)\;=\;\{\,x\in\mathcal{X}\mid\forall\,U\in\tau,\;x\in U,\;\mu(U)>0\}

supp⁡(μ)\operatorname{supp}(\mu) is the closure of every region where μ\mu has positive measure, or equivalently, the complement of the union of all μ\mu-null open sets:

supp⁡(μ)=𝒳∖{⋃{U∈τ∣μ⁡(U)=0}}\operatorname{supp}(\mu)\;=\;\mathcal{X}\setminus\Bigl\{\,\bigcup\{\,U\in\tau\mid\mu(U)=0\}\Bigr\}
Lemma 2.2 (Ill-Defined Expectation of Conditional Probability).

For probability measure PXP_{X}, a PXP_{X}-measurable function P⁡(A∣X=x):𝒳→[0,1]P(A\mid X=x):\mathcal{X}\to[0,1] is the conditional probability of event AA given X=xX=x. For probability measure PX′P_{X}^{\prime} satisfying supp⁡(PX′)∖supp⁡(PX)≠∅\operatorname{supp}(P_{X}^{\prime})\setminus\operatorname{supp}(P_{X})\neq\varnothing, the expectation 𝔼PX′​[P⁡(A∣X=x)]\mathbb{E}_{P_{X}^{\prime}}[P(A\mid X=x)] is arbitrary.

Remark

This problem arises because the conditional probability P⁡(A∣X=x)P(A\mid X=x) is unique almost everywhere with respect to PXP_{X} (unique PXP_{X}-a.e.), rather than to PX′P_{X}^{\prime}. When supp⁡(PX′)∖supp⁡(PX)≠∅\operatorname{supp}(P_{X}^{\prime})\setminus\operatorname{supp}(P_{X})\neq\varnothing, PX′P_{X}^{\prime} assigns positive mass to some PXP_{X}-null sets. In this case, 𝔼PX′​[P⁡(A∣X=x)]\mathbb{E}_{P_{X}^{\prime}}[P(A\mid X=x)] depends on the values of P⁡(A∣X=x)P(A\mid X=x) on sets where it is not uniquely determined. Hence, support mismatch leads to the ill-defined expectation of conditional probability. This issue directly impacts the definition and computation of Y∣\midX shift in existing theories, since the Y∣\midX shift is typically formulated as an expectation over conditional labeling distributions or its collapsed labeling functions.

With deterministic labeling, Zhao et al. (2019) used ℋ\mathcal{H}-divergence (Ben-David et al., 2006) to derive an error bound for soft-label binary classification under X and Y∣\midX shifts:

Theorem 2.3 (Existing Learning Bound on Distribution Shift).

Let 𝒟XS,𝒟XT\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S},\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T} be the covariate distributions and fS,fT:𝒳→[0,1]f_{S},f_{T}:\mathcal{X}\to[0,1] be the labeling functions for the source and target domain. Using absolute error loss |⋅||\cdot|, for any hypothesis space ℋ⊆[0,1]𝒳\mathcal{H}\subseteq[0,1]^{\mathcal{X}} define:

ℋ~={sgn(|h(x)−h′(x)|−t)|h,h′∈ℋ,t∈[0,1]},\tilde{\mathcal{H}}=\bigl\{\operatorname{sgn}(|h(x)-h^{\prime}(x)|-t)\;\bigm|\;h,h^{\prime}\in\mathcal{H},\;t\in[0,1]\bigr\},

then for any h∈ℋh\in\mathcal{H},

ϵT​(h)\displaystyle\epsilon_{T}(h) ≤ϵS(h)+dℋ~(𝒟XS,𝒟XT)+min{𝔼x∼𝒟XS[|fS(x)\displaystyle\;\leq\;\epsilon_{S}(h)+d_{\tilde{\mathcal{H}}}\!\bigl(\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S},\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}\bigr)+\min\Bigl\{\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S}}\bigl[\,|f_{S}(x)
−fT(x)|],𝔼x∼𝒟XT[|fS(x)−fT(x)|]}\displaystyle\qquad-f_{T}(x)|\,\bigr],\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}}\bigl[\,|f_{S}(x)-f_{T}(x)|\,\bigr]\Bigr\} (1)

Here, dℋ~d_{\tilde{\mathcal{H}}} measures X shift, and the two expectations 𝔼x∼𝒟XS​[|fS​(x)−fT​(x)|]\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S}}[|f_{S}(x)-f_{T}(x)|], 𝔼x∼𝒟XT​[|fS​(x)−fT​(x)|]\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}}[|f_{S}(x)-f_{T}(x)|] are both Y∣\midX shift but measured with the source or target covariate distribution, with the smaller one taken in the bound.

Remark* (Limitations of Theorem 2.3)

First, it is highly specialized, applying only to deterministic labeling, binary classification, and absolute loss. Moreover, when X shift causes support mismatch : supp⁡(𝒟XT)∖supp⁡(𝒟XS)≠∅\operatorname{supp}(\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T})\setminus\operatorname{supp}(\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S})\neq\varnothing, the conditional distribution 𝒟Y|X=xS\mathcal{D}_{Y|X=x}^{S} (i.e., fS​(x)f_{S}(x)) is only unique 𝒟XS\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S}-a.e. and arbitrary on the mismatched region, so the Y∣\midX shift 𝔼x∼𝒟XT​[|fS​(x)−fT​(x)|]\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}}[|f_{S}(x)-f_{T}(x)|] is ill-defined. Similarly, if supp⁡(𝒟XS)∖supp⁡(𝒟XT)≠∅\operatorname{supp}(\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S})\setminus\operatorname{supp}(\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T})\neq\varnothing, the other Y∣\midX shift term is also ill-defined. This additionally causes two problems:

  • •

    Loose bound. The ill-defined Y|XY|X shifts can take arbitrary values, making the bound in Eq. (1) loose.

  • •

    Non-estimable. When the real concept 𝒟Y|X=xS\mathcal{D}_{Y|X=x}^{S} or fS​(x)f_{S}(x) is unknown, we cannot sample it outside supp⁡(𝒟XS)\operatorname{supp}(\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S}); hence, under support mismatch the expectations 𝔼x∼𝒟XT​[|fS​(x)−fT​(x)|]\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}}\!\bigl[|f_{S}(x)-f_{T}(x)|\bigr] is non-estimable, as well as 𝔼x∼𝒟XS​[|fS​(x)−fT​(x)|]\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S}}\!\bigl[|f_{S}(x)-f_{T}(x)|\bigr].

2.3 Entropic Optimal Transport

We introduce entropic optimal transport, which we will employ to give the general definitions of X and Y∣\midX shifts properly. It measures the distance between two probability distributions, augmenting conventional optimal transport with a relative-entropy regularizer. Given two probability distributions ℙ\mathbb{P} and ℚ\mathbb{Q} on the metric space (Ω,ρ)(\Omega,\rho) and a parameter β≥0\beta\geq 0, the order-1 entropic optimal transport is:

Wβ​(ℙ,ℚ)\displaystyle W_{\beta}(\mathbb{P},\mathbb{Q}) =infγ∈Γ⁡(ℙ,ℚ){∫ρ​𝑑γ+β​H​(γ|ℙ⊗ℚ)}\displaystyle=\inf_{\gamma\in\Gamma(\mathbb{P},\mathbb{Q})}\biggl\{\int\rho\,d\gamma+\beta\,H\bigl(\gamma\bigm|\mathbb{P}\otimes\mathbb{Q}\bigr)\biggr\} (2)

where H⁡(γ|ℙ⊗ℚ)=∫log⁡(d​γ​(x1,x2)d​ℙ​(x1)​d​ℚ​(x2))​𝑑γ​(x1,x2)H\!\bigl(\gamma\bigm|\mathbb{P}\otimes\mathbb{Q}\bigr)\!=\!\int\log\Bigl(\tfrac{d\gamma(x_{1},x_{2})}{d\mathbb{P}(x_{1})\,d\mathbb{Q}(x_{2})}\Bigr)\,d\gamma(x_{1},x_{2}). Here, ρ⁡(x1,x2)\rho(x_{1},x_{2}) is the cost of transporting mass between points, Γ⁡(ℙ,ℚ)\Gamma(\mathbb{P},\mathbb{Q}) is the set of joint distributions with marginals ℙ\mathbb{P} and ℚ\mathbb{Q}, and γ⁡(x1,x2)\gamma(x_{1},x_{2}) is a transport coupling. Hence, Wβ​(ℙ,ℚ)W_{\beta}(\mathbb{P},\mathbb{Q}) is the minimum total transport cost between ℙ\mathbb{P} and ℚ\mathbb{Q} under an entropy regularizer. When β=0\beta=0, this reduces to the Wasserstein-1 distance, denoted by W1​(ℙ,ℚ)W_{1}(\mathbb{P},\mathbb{Q}). Compared with other distribution distances, (entropic) optimal transport has a well-established geometric meaning (Gangbo and McCann, 1996), and we will consistently use it to measure distribution shifts.

3 Theoretical Results

In this section, we focus on population-level theoretical results. We assume that covariate XX and label YY are distributed on the metric spaces (𝒳,ρ𝒳)(\mathcal{X},\rho_{\mathcal{X}}) and (𝒴,ρ𝒴)(\mathcal{Y},\rho_{\mathcal{Y}}), respectively, and give the rigorous and general definitions of their distribution shifts and essential theorems below.

3.1 General X and Y∣\midX Shifts

Definition 3.1 (X Shift).

Using entropic optimal transport, the X (covariate) shift is defined as:

SC​o​v\displaystyle S_{Cov} =Wβ(𝒟XS,𝒟XT)=infγ∈Γ⁡(𝒟XS,𝒟XT){∫ρ𝒳(xS,xT)\displaystyle=W_{\beta}\!\bigl(\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S},\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}\bigr)=\inf_{\gamma\in\Gamma(\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S},\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T})}\Bigl\{\int\rho_{\mathcal{X}}(x_{S},x_{T})\,
dγ(xS,xT)+βH(γ|𝒟XS⊗𝒟XT)}\displaystyle\qquad d\gamma(x_{S},x_{T})+\beta\,H\bigl(\gamma\bigm|\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S}\otimes\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}\bigr)\Bigr\} (3)

where the optimal coupling is denoted as γ∗\gamma^{*}, a joint distribution of 𝒟XS\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S}, 𝒟XT\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T} that gives the minimum transport cost.

With realistic stochastic labeling, the label follows a conditional distribution given the covariate; we give a general and rigorous definition of Y∣\midX shift below:

Definition 3.2 (γ∗\gamma^{*}-Y∣\midX Shift).

Let γ∗\gamma^{*} be the optimal transport coupling as in Definition 3.1, Sp​a​i​r​(xS,xT)=W1​(𝒟Y|X=xSS,𝒟Y|X=xTT)S_{pair}(x_{S},x_{T})=W_{1}\bigl(\mathcal{D}_{Y|X=x_{S}}^{S},\mathcal{D}_{Y|X=x_{T}}^{T}\bigr), then the γ∗\gamma^{*}-Y∣\midX shift is defined as the expectation of Sp​a​i​r​(xS,xT)S_{pair}(x_{S},x_{T}) under γ∗\gamma^{*}:

SC​p​tγ∗\displaystyle S_{Cpt}^{\gamma^{*}} =𝔼(xS,xT)∼γ∗​[Sp​a​i​r​(xS,xT)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{(x_{S},x_{T})\sim\gamma^{*}}\bigl[S_{pair}(x_{S},x_{T})\bigr]
=∫W1​(𝒟Y|X=xSS,𝒟Y|X=xTT)​d​γ∗​(xS,xT)\displaystyle=\int W_{1}\bigl(\mathcal{D}_{Y|X=x_{S}}^{S},\mathcal{D}_{Y|X=x_{T}}^{T}\bigr)\,d\gamma^{*}(x_{S},x_{T}) (4)

This definition is based on the optimal transport coupling γ∗\gamma^{*} for X shift. Sp​a​i​r​(xS,xT)S_{pair}(x_{S},x_{T}) denotes the paired conditional distribution shift between the source domain at xSx_{S} and the target domain at xTx_{T}. Intuitively, since optimal transport coupling γ∗\gamma^{*} places most of its mass on nearby pairs (xS,xT)(x_{S},x_{T}), SC​p​tγ∗S_{Cpt}^{\gamma^{*}} is evaluated mainly on such neighboring points.

With deterministic labeling, this definition reduces to:

Corollary 3.3 (Consistency under Deterministic Labeling).

Assume deterministic labeling 𝒟Y|X=xS=δfS​(x)\mathcal{D}_{Y|X=x}^{S}=\delta_{f_{S}(x)}, 𝒟Y|X=xT=δfT​(x)\mathcal{D}_{Y|X=x}^{T}=\delta_{f_{T}(x)}, then:

SC​p​tγ∗=𝔼γ∗​[Sp​a​i​r​(xS,xT)]=𝔼γ∗​[ρ𝒴​(fS​(xS),fT​(xT))]\displaystyle S_{Cpt}^{\gamma^{*}}=\mathbb{E}_{\gamma^{*}}\bigl[S_{pair}(x_{S},x_{T})\bigr]=\mathbb{E}_{\gamma^{*}}\bigl[\rho_{\mathcal{Y}}(f_{S}(x_{S}),f_{T}(x_{T}))\bigr]

The following three lemmas guarantee the good properties of γ∗\gamma^{*}-Y∣\midX Shift.

Lemma 3.4 (Support of γ∗\gamma^{*}).

For any γ∈Γ⁡(𝒟XS,𝒟XT)\gamma\in\Gamma(\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S},\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}), supp⁡(γ)⊆supp⁡(𝒟XS)×supp⁡(𝒟XT)\operatorname{supp}(\gamma)\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S})\times\operatorname{supp}(\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}).

Lemma 3.5 (Uniqueness of γ∗\gamma^{*}).

If β>0\beta>0, then the entropic optimal transport coupling γ∗\gamma^{*} in Definition 3.1 is unique.

Lemma 3.6 (Collapse of γ∗\gamma^{*}).

If β=0\beta=0 and 𝒟XS=𝒟XT\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S}=\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}, γ∗\gamma^{*} collapses to diagonal (identity) coupling γ∗=(Id,Id)#​𝒟XS\gamma^{*}=(\mathrm{Id},\mathrm{Id})_{\#}\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S}, equivalently, for every measurable A⊆𝒳×𝒳A\subseteq\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X}, γ∗(A)=∫𝟏{(x,x)∈A}d𝒟XS(x)\gamma^{*}(A)=\int\mathbf{1}_{\{(x,x)\in A\}}\,d\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S}(x), where 𝟏{⋅}\mathbf{1}_{\{\cdot\}} is the indicator function.

Combining Lemmas 3.4 and  3.5, the rigor of γ∗\gamma^{*}-Y∣\midX Shift is ensured:

Theorem 3.7 (Well-Definedness of γ∗\gamma^{*}-Y∣\midX Shift).

For β>0\beta>0, the γ∗\gamma^{*}-Y∣\midX shift SC​p​tγ∗S_{Cpt}^{\gamma^{*}} in Definition 3.2 is unique even when supp⁡(𝒟XS)≠supp⁡(𝒟XT)\operatorname{supp}(\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S})\neq\operatorname{supp}(\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}).

Remark

Such γ∗\gamma^{*}-Y∣\midX shift not only avoids the ill-definition encountered by existing theory, but also makes Y∣\midX shift tight and estimable. On the other hand, combining Corollary 3.3 and Lemma 3.6, the relationship between γ∗\gamma^{*}-Y∣\midX shift and existing Y∣\midX shift is shown as follows:

Proposition 3.8 (Relationship to existing Y∣\midX shift).

Assume deterministic labeling 𝒟Y|X=xS=δfS​(x)\mathcal{D}_{Y|X=x}^{S}=\delta_{f_{S}(x)}, 𝒟Y|X=xT=δfT​(x)\mathcal{D}_{Y|X=x}^{T}=\delta_{f_{T}(x)} and 𝒴⊂ℝ\mathcal{Y}\subset\mathbb{R} with ρ𝒴=|⋅|\rho_{\mathcal{Y}}=|\cdot|, if β=0\beta=0 and 𝒟XS=𝒟XT\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S}=\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}, then:

SC​p​tγ∗\displaystyle S_{Cpt}^{\gamma^{*}} =𝔼x∼𝒟XS​[|fS​(x)−fT​(x)|]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S}}\!\bigl[|f_{S}(x)-f_{T}(x)|\bigr]
=𝔼x∼𝒟XT​[|fS​(x)−fT​(x)|]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}}\!\bigl[|f_{S}(x)-f_{T}(x)|\bigr]

Remark

The above γ∗\gamma^{*}-Y∣\midX shift, defined via the entropic optimal transport coupling γ∗\gamma^{*}, applies to general settings including stochastic labeling. When 𝒟XS=𝒟XT\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S}=\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}, it recovers the existing Y∣\midX shift; and when the supports of 𝒟XS\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S} and 𝒟XT\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T} are mismatched, it still remains rigorous.

3.2 General Learning Bound

We now give a new cross-domain learning error bound based on X and γ∗\gamma^{*}-Y∣\midX shift. To be general, the output space of the learner is a metric space (𝒴′,ρ𝒴′)(\mathcal{Y}^{\prime},\rho_{\mathcal{Y}}^{\prime}), possibly different from the true label space (𝒴,ρ𝒴)(\mathcal{Y},\rho_{\mathcal{Y}}). For the loss function ℓ:𝒴×𝒴′→ℝ\ell:\mathcal{Y}\times\mathcal{Y}^{\prime}\to\mathbb{R}, we require the following basic assumption from them:

Assumption 3.9 (Separately Lipschitz Continuity).

For metric spaces (𝒴,ρ𝒴)(\mathcal{Y},\rho_{\mathcal{Y}}) and (𝒴′,ρ𝒴′)(\mathcal{Y}^{\prime},\rho_{\mathcal{Y}}^{\prime}), a function ℓ:𝒴×𝒴′→ℝ\ell:\mathcal{Y}\times\mathcal{Y}^{\prime}\to\mathbb{R} satisfies separately (Lℓ,Lℓ′)(L_{\ell},L_{\ell}^{\prime})-Lipschitz if there exist Lℓ,Lℓ′≥0L_{\ell},L_{\ell}^{\prime}\geq 0 such that for any y1,y2∈𝒴y_{1},y_{2}\in\mathcal{Y} and y1′,y2′∈𝒴′y_{1}^{\prime},y_{2}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}^{\prime}, there is:

|ℓ⁡(y1,y1′)−ℓ⁡(y2,y2′)|≤Lℓ​ρ𝒴​(y1,y2)+Lℓ′​ρ𝒴′​(y1′,y2′)\bigl|\ell(y_{1},y_{1}^{\prime})-\ell(y_{2},y_{2}^{\prime})\bigr|\!\leq\!L_{\ell}\,\rho_{\mathcal{Y}}(y_{1},y_{2})+L_{\ell}^{\prime}\,\rho_{\mathcal{Y}}^{\prime}(y_{1}^{\prime},y_{2}^{\prime}) (5)

Remark

This is a mild assumption: most loss functions are differentiable, which already implies continuity. And their stable optimization usually needs bounded gradients in a region, further ensuring Lipschitz continuity (Boyd and Vandenberghe, 2004). Note that this assumption also covers asymmetric losses. For instance, for binary classification with label space [0,1][0,1], output space is typically [a,1−a][a,1-a] (a∈(0,0.5)a\in(0,0.5)) by Sigmoid function and ρ𝒴=ρ𝒴′=|⋅|\rho_{\mathcal{Y}}=\rho_{\mathcal{Y}}^{\prime}=|\cdot|, the cross-entropy loss: ℓC​E​(y,y^)=−y​log⁡y^−(1−y)​log⁡(1−y^)\ell_{CE}(y,\hat{y})=-\,y\log\hat{y}\;-\;(1-y)\log(1-\hat{y}) satisfies separately (Lℓ,Lℓ′)(L_{\ell},L_{\ell}^{\prime})-Lipschitz with Lℓ=log⁡(1−aa)L_{\ell}=\log\bigl(\tfrac{1-a}{a}\bigr) and Lℓ′=1aL_{\ell}^{\prime}=\tfrac{1}{a}.

Corollary 3.10 (Composition Preserves Separate Lipschitzness).

Let h:𝒳→𝒴′h:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}^{\prime} be LhL_{h}-Lipschitz and let ℓ:𝒴×𝒴′→ℝ\ell:\mathcal{Y}\times\mathcal{Y}^{\prime}\to\mathbb{R} be separately (Lℓ,Lℓ′)(L_{\ell},L^{\prime}_{\ell})-Lipschitz. Then composite function ℓ⁡(y,h⁡(x)):𝒴×𝒳→ℝ\ell\bigl(y,h(x)\bigr):\mathcal{Y}\times\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R} is separately (Lℓ,Lh​Lℓ′)(L_{\ell},\,L_{h}L^{\prime}_{\ell})-Lipschitz.

The following two lemmas characterize the transport coupling of joint distributions 𝒟X​YS\mathcal{D}_{XY}^{S} and 𝒟X​YT\mathcal{D}_{XY}^{T}:

Lemma 3.11 (Separately Weak Duality).

Let 𝒢⁡(y,x):𝒴×𝒳→ℝ\mathcal{G}\bigl(y,x\bigr):\mathcal{Y}\times\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R} is separately (L𝒴,L𝒳)(L_{\mathcal{Y}},\,L_{\mathcal{X}})-Lipschitz, for any coupling of joint distributions γX​Y∈Γ(𝒟X​YS,𝒟X​YT)\gamma_{{}_{XY}}\in\Gamma(\mathcal{D}_{XY}^{S},\mathcal{D}_{XY}^{T}), there exists:

|𝔼𝒟X​YS[𝒢]]−𝔼𝒟X​YT[𝒢]|≤L𝒳EγX​Y[ρ𝒳]+L𝒴EγX​Y[ρ𝒴]\bigl|\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}_{XY}^{S}}\bigl[\mathcal{G}\bigr]\bigr]-\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}_{XY}^{T}}\bigl[\mathcal{G}\bigr]\bigr|\leq L_{\mathcal{X}}E_{\gamma_{{}_{XY}}}\bigl[\rho_{\mathcal{X}}\bigr]+L_{\mathcal{Y}}E_{\gamma_{{}_{XY}}}\bigl[\rho_{\mathcal{Y}}\bigr] (6)
Lemma 3.12 (Gluing Construction for Joint Coupling).

Let γ∗\gamma^{*} be the optimal transport coupling of X shift in Definition 3.1, γY|(xS,xT)∗\gamma^{*}_{Y|(x_{S},x_{T})} be the optimal transport coupling of Sp​a​i​r​(xS,xT)S_{pair}(x_{S},x_{T}) in Definition 3.2, construct the joint distribution of couplings: γX​Y(dxS,dxT,dyS,dyT)=γ∗(dxS,dxT)γY|(xS,xT)∗(dyS,dyT)\gamma_{{}_{XY}}(dx_{S},dx_{T},dy_{S},dy_{T})=\gamma^{*}(dx_{S},dx_{T})\gamma^{*}_{Y|(x_{S},x_{T})}(dy_{S},dy_{T}), then γX​Y\gamma_{{}_{XY}} is the coupling of joint distributions: γX​Y∈Γ(𝒟X​YS,𝒟X​YT)\gamma_{{}_{XY}}\in\Gamma(\mathcal{D}_{XY}^{S},\mathcal{D}_{XY}^{T}).

Combining Corollary 3.10, Lemmas 3.11 and  3.12, we obtain the general cross-domain error bound as follows:

Theorem 3.13 (General Learning Bound).

Given the covariate space (𝒳,ρ𝒳)(\mathcal{X},\rho_{\mathcal{X}}), the label space (𝒴,ρ𝒴)(\mathcal{Y},\rho_{\mathcal{Y}}), and the output space (𝒴′,ρ𝒴′)(\mathcal{Y}^{\prime},\rho_{\mathcal{Y}}^{\prime}), the source and target distributions are (𝒟XS,𝒟Y|X=xS)(\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S},\mathcal{D}_{Y|X=x}^{S}) and (𝒟XT,𝒟Y|X=xT)(\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T},\mathcal{D}_{Y|X=x}^{T}), respectively. If the loss ℓ:𝒴×𝒴′→ℝ\ell:\mathcal{Y}\times\mathcal{Y}^{\prime}\to\mathbb{R} satisfies separately (Lℓ,Lℓ′)(L_{\ell},L_{\ell}^{\prime})-Lipschitz, then for any hypothesis h:𝒳→𝒴′h:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}^{\prime} that satisfies LhL_{h}-Lipschitz, the following bound holds:

ϵT​(h)≤ϵS​(h)+Lh​Lℓ′​SC​o​v+Lℓ​SC​p​tγ∗\epsilon_{T}(h)\;\leq\;\epsilon_{S}(h)\;+\;L_{h}\,L_{\ell}^{\prime}\,S_{Cov}\;+\;L_{\ell}\,S_{Cpt}^{\gamma^{*}} (7)

where SC​o​vS_{Cov} is the X shift in Definition 3.1 and SC​p​tγ∗S_{Cpt}^{\gamma^{*}} is the γ∗\gamma^{*}-Y∣\midX shift in Definition 3.2.

Remark

This elegant bound unifies the covariate shift SC​o​vS_{Cov} and the concept shift (γ∗\gamma^{*}-Y∣\midX shift) SC​p​tγ∗S_{Cpt}^{\gamma^{*}}’s effect on target error via the Lipschitz factors Lh​Lℓ′L_{h}\,L_{\ell}^{\prime} and LℓL_{\ell}. Notably, it depends only on the Lipschitz continuity of the hypothesis hh and the loss ℓ\ell, without any other specific restriction on the label space 𝒴\mathcal{Y} or loss ℓ\ell. It naturally covers binary classification or regression tasks when 𝒴\mathcal{Y} is one-dimensional, and multiclass classification or multi-label tasks when 𝒴\mathcal{Y} is multi-dimensional. Besides, since the bound holds under stochastic labeling, it applies to a wide range of supervised learning scenarios in practice. On the other hand, by using the well-defined γ∗\gamma^{*}-Y∣\midX shift, our bound can be tighter than the existing bound, and more crucially, both the covariate and concept shifts in our theory can be robustly estimated from the finite samples. Additionally, since the entropic optimal transport SC​o​vS_{Cov} increases with the hyperparameter β\beta, we recommend choosing β\beta as a small non-zero value to balance the tightness and the rigor of the theory.

4 Statistical Results

In practice, true domain distributions are all unknown. We wish to estimate the shifts from domain samples and analyze how these shifts will influence model performance. In this section, we focus on sample-level theoretical results. Suppose we have i.i.d. samples {(Xi(S),Yi(S))}\{(X_{i}^{(S)},Y_{i}^{(S)})\} and {(Xj(T),Yj(T))}\{(X_{j}^{(T)},Y_{j}^{(T)})\} drawn from 𝒟X​YS\mathcal{D}_{XY}^{S} and 𝒟X​YT\mathcal{D}_{XY}^{T} with sizes NSN_{S} and NTN_{T}, respectively. This section involves three parts: the estimation of X shift, the estimation of Y∣\midX shift, and the DataShifts algorithm to estimate the overall bound.

4.1 Estimation of X Shift

By Definition 3.1, the X shift is the entropic optimal transport between 𝒟XS\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S} and 𝒟XT\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}. The traditional estimation method uses the entropic optimal transport of empirical distributions—known as the plug-in estimator.

Traditional Plug-in Estimator

Given i.i.d. samples {Xi(S)}∼𝒟XS\{X_{i}^{(S)}\}\sim\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S}, {Xj(T)}∼𝒟XT\{X_{j}^{(T)}\}\sim\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T} with sample sizes NS,NTN_{S},N_{T} respectively, set the empirical measures: 𝒟XS^=1NS​∑i=1NSδXi(S)\widehat{\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S}}=\frac{1}{N_{S}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{S}}\delta_{X_{i}^{(S)}}, 𝒟XT^=1NT​∑j=1NTδXj(T)\widehat{\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}}=\frac{1}{N_{T}}\sum_{j=1}^{N_{T}}\delta_{X_{j}^{(T)}}, their entropic optimal transport is:

Wβ​(𝒟XS^,𝒟XT^)=minγ^⁡⟨C,γ^⟩+β​∑i=1NS∑j=1NTγ^i​j​log⁡γ^i​j\displaystyle W_{\beta}\bigl(\widehat{\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S}},\widehat{\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}}\bigr)=\min_{\hat{\gamma}}\,\langle C,\hat{\gamma}\rangle+\beta\sum_{i=1}^{N_{S}}\sum_{j=1}^{N_{T}}\hat{\gamma}_{ij}\,\log\hat{\gamma}_{ij}
+β​log⁡(NS​NT)s.t.γ^=1NS​𝟏,γ^⊤=1NT​𝟏\displaystyle+\beta\,\log\bigl(N_{S}N_{T}\bigr)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\hat{\gamma}\mathbf{1}\!=\!\tfrac{1}{N_{S}}\mathbf{1},\;\hat{\gamma}^{\top}\mathbf{1}\!=\!\tfrac{1}{N_{T}}\mathbf{1} (8)

where C∈ℝ+NS×NTC\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{N_{S}\times N_{T}} is the cost matrix with ci​j=ρ𝒳​(Xi(S),Xj(T))c_{ij}=\rho_{\mathcal{X}}\bigl(X_{i}^{(S)},X_{j}^{(T)}\bigr), and γ^∈ℝ+NS×NT\hat{\gamma}\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{N_{S}\times N_{T}} represents any discretized transport coupling satisfying the given linear constraints. Such an optimization problem can be solved efficiently at a large scale by the Sinkhorn algorithm (Cuturi, 2013; Genevay et al., 2016).

Curse of Dimensionality.

However, in modern applications, the covariate space 𝒳\mathcal{X} is often high-dimensional. Even when two distributions are very close, their samples’ distance can be large. Such curse of dimensionality makes the plug-in estimator greatly overestimated (Verleysen and François, 2005; Panaretos and Zemel, 2019) (Fig.1(a)). When β\beta is small, entropic optimal transport behaves similarly to Wasserstein distance (Carlier et al., 2017; Carlier et al., 2023), and the upward bias decays only in O(N−1/d)O(N^{-1/d}) order (Fournier and Guillin, 2015), which implies that increasing NN has a very limited debiasing effect when dd is high (Fig.1(b)).

To address the overestimation problem of the traditional plug-in estimator, we propose the following debiased estimator.

Definition 4.1 (Debiased Estimator).

Given i.i.d. samples {Xi(S)}∼𝒟XS\{X_{i}^{(S)}\}\sim\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S}, {Xj(T)}∼𝒟XT\{X_{j}^{(T)}\}\sim\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T} with sample sizes NS,NTN_{S},N_{T} respectively, split the samples in half to obtain four independent empirical measures: 𝒟XS^′=2NS​∑i=1NS/2δXi(S)\widehat{\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S}}^{\prime}=\frac{2}{N_{S}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{S}/2}\delta_{X_{i}^{(S)}}, 𝒟XS^′′=2NS​∑i=NS/2+1NSδXi(S)\widehat{\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S}}^{\prime\prime}=\frac{2}{N_{S}}\sum_{i=N_{S}/2+1}^{N_{S}}\delta_{X_{i}^{(S)}}, 𝒟XT^′=2NT​∑j=1NT/2δXj(T)\widehat{\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}}^{\prime}=\frac{2}{N_{T}}\sum_{j=1}^{N_{T}/2}\delta_{X_{j}^{(T)}}, 𝒟XT^′′=2NT​∑j=NT/2+1NTδXj(T)\widehat{\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}}^{\prime\prime}=\frac{2}{N_{T}}\sum_{j=N_{T}/2+1}^{N_{T}}\delta_{X_{j}^{(T)}}. The debiased estimator is:

Wβd​e​b\displaystyle W_{\beta}^{deb}\! (𝒟XS^,𝒟XT^)=|12​Wβ​(𝒟XS^′,𝒟XT^′)2+12​Wβ​(𝒟XS^′′,𝒟XT^′′)2\displaystyle\bigl(\widehat{\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S}},\widehat{\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}}\bigr)\!=\!\Biggl\lvert\tfrac{1}{2}W_{\beta}\!\bigl(\widehat{\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S}}^{\prime}\!,\widehat{\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}}^{\prime}\bigr)^{2}\!+\!\tfrac{1}{2}W_{\beta}\!\bigl(\widehat{\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S}}^{\prime\prime}\!,\widehat{\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}}^{\prime\prime}\bigr)^{2}
−\displaystyle- 12Wβ(𝒟XS^′,𝒟XS^′′)2−12Wβ(𝒟XT^′,𝒟XT^′′)2|1/2\displaystyle\tfrac{1}{2}W_{\beta}\!\bigl(\widehat{\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S}}^{\prime}\!,\widehat{\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S}}^{\prime\prime}\bigr)^{2}-\tfrac{1}{2}W_{\beta}\!\bigl(\widehat{\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}}^{\prime}\!,\widehat{\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}}^{\prime\prime}\bigr)^{2}\Biggr\rvert^{1/2} (9)

Remark

This debiased estimator uses four plug-in estimators. The first two terms, Wβ​(𝒟XS^′,𝒟XT^′)W_{\beta}\bigl(\widehat{\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S}}^{\prime},\widehat{\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}}^{\prime}\bigr) and Wβ​(𝒟XS^′′,𝒟XT^′′)W_{\beta}\bigl(\widehat{\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S}}^{\prime\prime},\widehat{\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}}^{\prime\prime}\bigr), estimate the distance between 𝒟XS\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S} and 𝒟XT\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}, including the sample bias. And the last two terms, Wβ​(𝒟XS^′,𝒟XS^′′)W_{\beta}\bigl(\widehat{\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S}}^{\prime},\widehat{\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S}}^{\prime\prime}\bigr) and Wβ​(𝒟XT^′,𝒟XT^′′)W_{\beta}\bigl(\widehat{\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}}^{\prime},\widehat{\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}}^{\prime\prime}\bigr) estimate the distance arising from sample bias only. Subtracting the two parts reduces the sample bias, thus giving a better estimate of Wβ​(𝒟XS,𝒟XT)W_{\beta}(\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S},\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}). Compared with the traditional plug-in estimator, our debiased estimator Wβd​e​bW_{\beta}^{deb} reduces the overestimation and remains accurate regardless of the true distribution distance (see Fig.1(a) and 1(c)).

Moreover, when the covariate space is Euclidean, we derived a concentration inequality guaranteeing that the debiased estimator converges to the true distance:

Theorem 4.2 (Concentration Inequality of Debiased Estimator).

Let 𝒟XS,𝒟XT\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S},\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T} be two distributions on (ℝd,∥⋅∥)(\mathbb{R}^{d},\|\cdot\|) with finite squared-exponential moments. For i.i.d. samples {Xi(S)}∼𝒟XS\{X_{i}^{(S)}\}\sim\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S}, {Xj(T)}∼𝒟XT\{X_{j}^{(T)}\}\sim\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T} with sample sizes NS,NTN_{S},N_{T} respectively, when β=0\beta=0, and for any ε>0\varepsilon>0, there exists NN such that if NS,NT>NN_{S},N_{T}>N, then:

ℙ⁡(|Wβd​e​b​(𝒟XS^,𝒟XT^)−Wβ​(𝒟XS,𝒟XT)|>ε)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\Bigl(\bigl|\,W_{\beta}^{deb}(\widehat{\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S}},\widehat{\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}})-W_{\beta}(\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S},\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T})\bigr|>\varepsilon\Bigr) ≤\displaystyle\leq
2​exp⁡(−λS​NS​Vε​ε232)+2​exp⁡(−λT​NT​Vε​ε232)\displaystyle\quad 2\exp\Bigl(-\tfrac{\lambda_{S}\,N_{S}\,V_{\varepsilon}\,\varepsilon^{2}}{32}\Bigr)+2\exp\Bigl(-\tfrac{\lambda_{T}\,N_{T}\,V_{\varepsilon}\,\varepsilon^{2}}{32}\Bigr) (10)

where λS,λT>0\lambda_{S},\lambda_{T}>0 depend only on squared-exponential moments of 𝒟XS,𝒟XT\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S},\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}, respectively, and Vε∈[2−3,2)V_{\varepsilon}\in[2-\sqrt{3},2) depends only on Wβ​(𝒟XS,𝒟XT)/εW_{\beta}(\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S},\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T})/\varepsilon.

Remark

This theorem implies that the deviation probability of the debiased estimator decays exponentially with sample sizes, so with high probability, our debiased estimator can well approximate the true entropic optimal transport distance Wβ​(𝒟XS,𝒟XT)W_{\beta}(\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S},\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}). Notably, it also shows the enlightening fact that our estimator’s concentration depends not only on each distribution’s scale characterized by λS,λT\lambda_{S},\lambda_{T} but also on the true distance between two distributions.

4.2 Estimation of Y∣\midX Shift

As above, we defined the γ∗\gamma^{*}-Y∣\midX shift SC​p​tγ∗S_{Cpt}^{\gamma^{*}} in Definition 3.2; we now estimate it from samples.

Definition 4.3 (Estimator for γ∗\gamma^{*}-Y∣\midX Shift).

Given i.i.d. samples {(Xi(S),Yi(S))}∼𝒟X​YS\{(X_{i}^{(S)},Y_{i}^{(S)})\}\sim\mathcal{D}_{XY}^{S}, {(Xj(T),Yj(T))}∼𝒟X​YT\{(X_{j}^{(T)},Y_{j}^{(T)})\}\sim\mathcal{D}_{XY}^{T} with sample sizes NS,NTN_{S},N_{T} respectively, the estimator of γ∗\gamma^{*}-Y∣\midX shift is defined as:

S^C​p​t=∑i=1NS∑j=1NTρ𝒴​(Yi(S),Yj(T))​γ^i​j∗,\hat{S}_{Cpt}=\sum_{i=1}^{N_{S}}\sum_{j=1}^{N_{T}}\rho_{\mathcal{Y}}\bigl(Y_{i}^{(S)},Y_{j}^{(T)}\bigr)\,\hat{\gamma}_{ij}^{*}, (11)

where γ^∗∈ℝ+NS×NT\hat{\gamma}^{*}\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{N_{S}\times N_{T}} represents the discrete optimal transport coupling for Wβ​(𝒟XS^,𝒟XT^)W_{\beta}(\widehat{\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S}},\widehat{\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}}).

Remark

In Section 4.1, we use the debiased estimator Wβd​e​b​(𝒟XS^,𝒟XT^)W_{\beta}^{deb}\!\bigl(\widehat{\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S}},\widehat{\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}}\bigr) for X shift, whereas Definition 4.3 still estimates γ∗\gamma^{*}-Y∣\midX shift via the optimal transport coupling from the plug-in estimator Wβ​(𝒟XS^,𝒟XT^)W_{\beta}(\widehat{\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S}},\widehat{\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}}). This is because the curse of dimensionality mainly affects the transport cost (i.e., inter-sample distances), rather than the transport coupling. Leveraging the stability of entropic optimal transport (Eckstein and Nutz, 2022), the following lemma establishes the convergence of the coupling for plug-in estimator:

Lemma 4.4 (Stability of Entropic Optimal Transport Coupling).

Let 𝒟XS,𝒟XT\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S},\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T} be two distributions on (𝒳,ρ𝒳)(\mathcal{X},\rho_{\mathcal{X}}) with finite squared-exponential moments. γ∗\gamma^{*} and γ^∗\hat{\gamma}^{*} are the optimal transport couplings of Wβ​(𝒟XS,𝒟XT)W_{\beta}(\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S},\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}) and Wβ​(𝒟XS^,𝒟XT^)W_{\beta}(\widehat{\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S}},\widehat{\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}}) respectively, then:

W1​(γ∗,γ^∗)≤Λ+2​2β​λγ∗​Λ\displaystyle W_{1}\left(\gamma^{*},\hat{\gamma}^{*}\right)\leq\varLambda+2\sqrt{\frac{2}{\beta\lambda_{\gamma^{*}}}}\sqrt{\varLambda}
Λ=W1​(𝒟XS,𝒟XS^)+W1​(𝒟XT,𝒟XT^)\displaystyle\varLambda=W_{1}\left(\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S},\widehat{\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S}}\right)+W_{1}\left(\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T},\widehat{\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}}\right) (12)

where W1​(γ∗,γ^∗)W_{1}\left(\gamma^{*},\hat{\gamma}^{*}\right) is computed on 𝒳×𝒳\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X} with metric ρ⁡((x1,x2),(x1′,x2′)):=ρ𝒳​(x1,x1′)+ρ𝒳​(x2,x2′)\rho\big((x_{1},x_{2}),(x_{1}^{\prime},x_{2}^{\prime})\big):=\rho_{\mathcal{X}}(x_{1},x_{1}^{\prime})+\rho_{\mathcal{X}}(x_{2},x_{2}^{\prime}), λγ∗>0\lambda_{\gamma^{*}}>0 depend only on squared-exponential moments of 𝒟XS,𝒟XT\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S},\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}.

Remark

This lemma shows that the Wasserstein-11 distance between the plug-in estimator coupling and the population optimal transport coupling, is bounded by the sum of the marginal Wasserstein-11 distance between each population and its empirical distribution, with the bound scaled by the parameter β\beta. Such a uniform bound is guaranteed only when β>0\beta>0, which further highlights the necessity of using entropic optimal transport.

By Lemma 4.4, when covariate space 𝒳\mathcal{X} is Euclidean and label space 𝒴\mathcal{Y} is a bounded set in an Euclidean space, we derive a concentration inequality guaranteeing estimator in Definition 4.3 approximates true value:

Theorem 4.5 (Concentration Inequality for Definition 4.3).

Let 𝒟XS,𝒟XT\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S},\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T} be two distributions on (ℝd,∥⋅∥)(\mathbb{R}^{d},\|\cdot\|) with finite squared-exponential moments. Let the label space 𝒴⊂ℝd​’\mathcal{Y}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d’} be bounded by M=supy,y′∈𝒴‖y−y′‖M=\sup_{y,y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}}\|\,y-y^{\prime}\|, on which conditional distributions 𝒟Y|X=xSS,𝒟Y|X=xTT\mathcal{D}_{Y|X=x_{S}}^{S},\mathcal{D}_{Y|X=x_{T}}^{T} satisfy LY|XL_{Y|X}-Lipschitz respectively: dTV​(𝒟Y|X=x,𝒟Y|X=x′)≤LY|X​‖x−x′‖d_{\mathrm{TV}}\bigl(\mathcal{D}_{Y|X=x},\mathcal{D}_{Y|X=x^{\prime}}\bigr)\;\leq\;L_{Y|X}\,\|\,x-x^{\prime}\|. For i.i.d. samples {(Xi(S),Yi(S))}∼𝒟X​YS\{(X_{i}^{(S)},Y_{i}^{(S)})\}\sim\mathcal{D}_{XY}^{S}, {(Xj(T),Yj(T))}∼𝒟X​YT\{(X_{j}^{(T)},Y_{j}^{(T)})\}\sim\mathcal{D}_{XY}^{T} with sample sizes NS,NTN_{S},N_{T}, when β>0\beta>0, and for any ε>0\varepsilon>0, there exists NN such that if NS,NT>NN_{S},N_{T}>N, then:

ℙ⁡(CLOSE\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\bigl( OPEN|S^C​p​t−SC​p​tγ∗−Δ|>ε)≤2​exp⁡(−NS​NT​Φ​ε2(NS+NT)​M2)\displaystyle|\hat{S}_{Cpt}-S_{Cpt}^{\gamma^{*}}-\varDelta|\!>\!\varepsilon\bigr)\leq 2\exp\Bigl(-\frac{N_{S}\,N_{T}\,\varPhi\,\varepsilon^{2}}{(N_{S}+N_{T})M^{2}}\Bigr)
+exp⁡(−λS1/2​NS​Φ​ε24​λT1/2​M2)+exp⁡(−λT1/2​NT​Φ​ε24​λS1/2​M2)\displaystyle+\!\exp\Bigl(-\frac{\lambda_{S}^{1/2}N_{S}\varPhi\,\varepsilon^{2}}{4\,\lambda_{T}^{1/2}M^{2}}\Bigr)\!+\exp\Bigl(-\frac{\lambda_{T}^{1/2}N_{T}\,\varPhi\,\varepsilon^{2}}{4\,\lambda_{S}^{1/2}M^{2}}\Bigr) (13)

where dTVd_{\mathrm{TV}} is total-variation distance, λS,λT>0\lambda_{S},\lambda_{T}>0 depend only on the squared-exponential moments of 𝒟XS,𝒟XT\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S},\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}, Φ>0\varPhi>0 depends on LY|X,λS,λT,βL_{Y|X},\lambda_{S},\lambda_{T},\beta, the bias Δ\varDelta is a constant.

Remark

This theorem implies that the deviation probability of the γ∗\gamma^{*}-Y∣\midX Shift estimator S^C​p​t\hat{S}_{Cpt} decays exponentially with sample sizes, so with high probability, the estimator can well approximate the SC​p​tγ∗+ΔS_{Cpt}^{\gamma^{*}}\!+\!\varDelta. The bias term Δ\varDelta arises because Definition 4.3 uses ρ𝒴​(Yi(S),Yj(T))\rho_{\mathcal{Y}}\!\bigl(Y_{i}^{(S)},Y_{j}^{(T)}\bigr) as a single-point estimate of Sp​a​i​r​(Xi(S),Xj(T))S_{pair}\bigl(X_{i}^{(S)},X_{j}^{(T)}\bigr) in Definition 3.2. The following two propositions show that the bias Δ\varDelta is controlled.

Proposition 4.6 (Δ\varDelta in Deterministic Labeling).

Assume deterministic labeling 𝒟Y|X=xS=δfS​(x)\mathcal{D}_{Y|X=x}^{S}=\delta_{f_{S}(x)}, 𝒟Y|X=xT=δfT​(x)\mathcal{D}_{Y|X=x}^{T}=\delta_{f_{T}(x)}, then the Δ\varDelta in Theorem 4.5 satisfies:

Δ=0\varDelta=0 (14)

Remark

This proposition shows that under deterministic labeling, the estimator S^C​p​t\hat{S}_{Cpt} accurately estimates the Y∣\midX shift SC​p​tγ∗S_{Cpt}^{\gamma^{*}} itself. For stochastic labeling, we show that Δ\varDelta can be bounded by the irreducible error (James et al., 2013) (also known as the Bayes risk (Berger, 2013)) in traditional statistical learning.

Proposition 4.7 (Δ\varDelta in Stochastic Labeling).

When (𝒴,ρ𝒴)=(ℝd′,∥⋅∥)(\mathcal{Y},\rho_{\mathcal{Y}})=(\mathbb{R}^{d^{\prime}},\|\cdot\|), the irreducible error of joint distribution 𝒟X​Y\mathcal{D}_{XY} under squared loss ∥⋅∥2\|\cdot\|^{2} is defined as: I(𝒟X​Y)=infg:𝒳→𝒴𝔼(x,y)∼𝒟X​Y[∥y−g(x)∥2]\mathrm{I}(\mathcal{D}_{XY})=\inf_{g:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}}\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}_{XY}}\bigl[\|y-g(x)\|^{2}\bigr], then the Δ\varDelta in Theorem 4.5 satisfies:

0≤Δ≤I⁡(𝒟X​YS)+I⁡(𝒟X​YT)0\;\leq\;\varDelta\;\leq\;\sqrt{\mathrm{I}(\mathcal{D}_{XY}^{S})}\;+\;\sqrt{\mathrm{I}(\mathcal{D}_{XY}^{T})} (15)

Remark

The irreducible error is the fundamental error inherent to stochastic labeling that no model can overcome. When the problem is learnable, covariate and label are often well correlated, and the irreducible error is small relative to the overall label variability. In this case, Proposition 4.7 guarantees that the estimator S^C​p​t\hat{S}_{Cpt} does not substantially overestimate the Y∣\midX shift SC​p​tγ∗S_{Cpt}^{\gamma^{*}}.

4.3 DataShifts Algorithm

On the Lipschitz Constant of Learners.

The Lipschitz constant of the learner have been well studied, such as logistic regression (Roux et al., 2012), multi-layer perceptron (MLP) (Fazlyab et al., 2019), convolutional neural networks (CNN) (Virmaux and Scaman, 2018; Zou et al., 2019) and attention mechanism (Kim et al., 2021; Castin et al., 2023). Although the Lipschitz constants of modern large-scale neural networks such as ResNet-50 or Transformers remain difficult to analyze, researchers are more concerned with whether these models learn distribution-robust representations (Hendrycks et al., 2020), rather than distribution shift in the raw input space. In this setting, the covariate space 𝒳\mathcal{X} is the representation space, and the downstream model (the hypothesis hh in our theory) is often a simple learner—such as a linear classifier—whose Lipschitz constant is still easy to handle. We summarize the Lipschitz constants of various learners in Appendix D.

By leveraging the theoretical results above, we give the plug-and-play Algorithm 1 (DataShifts) for quantifying X and Y∣\midX shifts from finite samples and estimating error bounds.

5 Experiments

In this section, we apply our estimable general theory to three distinct practical tasks: tabular regression, image binary classification, and image multi-class classification – to validate the general effectiveness of our bound and estimators. We also conduct experiments on synthetic tasks where existing theory apply, demonstrating our bound is tighter.

5.1 Novozymes Enzyme Stability Prediction

The Novozymes Enzyme Prediction Competition (Pultz et al., 2022) is a large‐scale Kaggle contest. It is a tabular regression task, with 9,000 point-mutation samples spanning 180 enzyme families, aiming to predict transition temperatures for unseen families. Each enzyme family is treated as a separate domain; due to distribution shifts between them, thousands of participants found it difficult to develop any effective solution.

We select the 60 enzyme families with the smallest pretraining error as the source domain, and treat each of the remaining 120 enzyme families as a target domain. In this task, we focus on the distribution shift between the raw data of different enzyme families, taking the 20-dimensional input feature space as covariate space 𝒳\mathcal{X}. We train a 3-layer MLP on the source domain; an analysis of its Lipschitz constant is provided in the Appendix D.4. We use the absolute loss (separately (1,1)(1,1)-Lipschitz) to evaluate the source domain error and the test error on each target domain, and apply our DataShifts algorithm(β=0.2\beta=0.2) to estimate an error bound for each target domain.

We plot the test error and the estimated error bound on each target domain in Fig. 2(a). In this figure, the overall trend of the test error and the error bound lies just above the diagonal, indicating that our bound is tight and effectively captures the test error under distribution shift. Meanwhile, it directly shows the contributions of X and Y∣\midX shifts on the error bound. The large Y∣\midX shift across enzyme families is what drives the generalization failure in this contest.

5.2 ColoredMNIST and PACS

ColoredMNIST and PACS are two standard tasks in the DomainBed benchmark(Gulrajani and Lopez-Paz, 2020). ColoredMNIST is a binary classification task with 70,000 handwritten digit images exhibiting color shift, while PACS is a multi-class object recognition task with 9,991 images exhibiting style shift. For both tasks, we treat the model’s representation space as the covariate space 𝒳\mathcal{X}. Following the DomainBed setup, we use the simple CNN with a 128-dimensional representation for ColoredMNIST, and ResNet-50 with a 2048-dimensional representation for PACS. In this setting, the hypothesis hh in our theory corresponds to the model’s final layer (a linear classifier), whose Lipschitz constant is analyzed in the Appendix D.3.

We evaluate three methods: ERM, CORAL, and MMD. Adhering to DomainBed, we select the best hyperparameters via training-domain validation over 20 random hyperparameter trials for each method, domain, and trial. For ColoredMNIST, we train each best-hyperparameter run for 5,000 steps and save checkpoints every 100 steps. For PACS, since the model converges earlier, we train for 1,000 steps and save checkpoints every 20 steps. At each checkpoint, we regard the mixture distribution over training domains as the source domain and the test domain as the target domain. We still use the absolute loss to measure source and target errors, and run our DataShifts algorithm (β=0.2\beta=0.2) using each domain’s representation-label pairs to estimate the test domain error bound at every checkpoint.

We plot the test error and the estimated error bound for both tasks in Fig. 2(b) and 2(c). In Fig. 2(b), the bound tracks the test error well across checkpoints. The MMD (purple) and CORAL (yellow) points lie closer to the lower-left region, indicating that these X shift-reducing methods indeed yield smaller bounds, and consequently lower error on ColoredMNIST. In Fig. 2(c), although the bound becomes looser in magnitude when applied to PACS, a more complex image classification task, it still exhibits a consistent trend with the test error in each run.

5.3 Synthetic Binary Classification

We compare our theory with the existing bound in Zhao et al. (2019), which is shown to be tighter than previous learning bounds. As discussed in Remark*, the existing learning bound only applies to soft-label binary classification with deterministic labeling and absolute loss. Since its estimation requires sampling the true concepts fSf_{S} and fTf_{T} outside the supports of the covariate distributions 𝒟XS\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S}, 𝒟XT\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T} (oracle), it can only be estimated on synthetic tasks where the true concepts are known.

We construct a synthetic binary classification task using logistic regression. Let the covariate space be 10-dimensional, and the source inputs are sampled from standard normal distribution: 𝒟XS=𝒩⁡(𝟎,I)\mathcal{D}^{S}_{X}=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},I), with labels generated by fS​(x)=σ⁡(wS⊤​x+bS)f_{S}(x)=\sigma(w_{S}^{\top}x+b_{S}), where wS=𝟏/10w_{S}=\mathbf{1}/\sqrt{10}, bS=0b_{S}=0 and σ\sigma is the sigmoid function. The target inputs are generated by shifting 𝒟XS\mathcal{D}^{S}_{X} along a random direction, thereby controlling the X shift. And the target labels are generated by another logistic regression: fT​(x)=σ⁡(wT⊤​x+bT)f_{T}(x)=\sigma(w_{T}^{\top}x+b_{T}), where wTw_{T} is obtained by rotating wSw_{S} by angle θ\theta toward a random direction. θ\theta and bTb_{T} further control the Y∣\midX shift. By varying the X shift, θ\theta, and bTb_{T}, we obtain a series of target domains. We also use logistic regression as the learner and train it on the source domain. Its Lipschitz constant is analyzed in Appendix D.2. For each target domain, we estimate the test error, the existing and our bounds under the absolute loss.

We plot the learning bounds with respect to the X shift and the Y∣\midX shifts (θ\theta and bTb_{T}) in Fig. 3. In Fig. 3(a), since both the source concept and the learner are logistic regression models, the learner can fit the source concept well, and the X shift in the target domain has only a minor effect on the test error. As the X shift increases, our bound becomes tighter than the existing bound. In Figs. 3(b) and 3(c), as the Y∣\midX shift increases, the existing bound becomes looser than ours. This verifies our point in Remark*: the ill-defined Y∣\midX shift in the existing bound is loose, whereas our γ∗\gamma^{*}-Y∣\midX shift and the accompanying learning bound can be tighter.

In addition to the above results, sensitivity experiments of the proposed estimators with respect to the parameter β\beta are provided in Appendix E.1. Experiments on the bias of the γ∗\gamma^{*}-Y∣\midX shift estimator under stochastic labeling are presented in Appendix E.2.

6 Conclusion

In this paper, we focus on a general and estimable theoretical framework for learning under distribution shift. We first introduce a key notion, γ∗\gamma^{*}-Y∣\midX shift, via entropic optimal transport, which addresses the ill-definedness in existing theory. Then we derive a general learning bound unifying X shift and γ∗\gamma^{*}-Y∣\midX shift. We further develop concentration-guaranteed estimators for both shifts, and integrate our theory into the plug-and-play DataShifts algorithm, enabling researchers to quantify and analyze distribution shift in broad settings. Experiments on practical and synthetic tasks validate the general effectiveness and tightness of our theory. We believe our theoretical framework takes an important step toward learning under distribution shift and will spur further algorithmic advances.

Appendix A Related Work

Generalization theory under distribution shift is an important and long-standing problem. Researchers usually seek to measure distribution shift using some distribution divergence and derive corresponding learning bounds. Early theoretical works mainly focused on the X (covariate) shift. Ben-David et al. (2006); Ben-David et al. (2010) used the ℋ\mathcal{H}-divergence to measure X shift between the source and target domains for binary classification, thereby deriving learning bounds for domain adaptation. Subsequent studies characterized the X shift via maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), leading to new learning bounds and improved domain adaptation algorithms (Long et al., 2015). Redko et al. (2017); Courty et al. (2017); Shen et al. (2018) adopted optimal transport (OT) to characterize X shift and obtained similar bounds. Further studies proposed more complex metrics for the X shift to extend the theory to multiclass classification (Zhang et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2020; El Hamri et al., 2025).

Most of these theories focus only on the X shift and follow a similar proof strategy, resulting in a joint error term between the source and target domains, λ=minh⁡ϵS​(h)+ϵT​(h)\lambda=\min_{h}\epsilon_{S}(h)+\epsilon_{T}(h), which is widely recognized as loose and non-estimable. Our baseline, Zhao et al. (2019), showed that the Y∣\midX (concept) shift is implicitly contained in this joint error term λ\lambda, and derived a tighter learning bound by explicitly introducing the Y∣\midX shift instead. Zhang et al. (2023) extended this theory to multiclass classification. We follow this path of explicitly characterizing the Y∣\midX shift, and point out that the existing definition of the Y∣\midX shift becomes ill-defined when the supports of the covariate distributions are mismatched, which still makes the Y∣\midX shift loose and non-estimable. Through entropic optimal transport, we introduce a well-defined γ∗\gamma^{*}-Y∣\midX shift and the corresponding learning bound, which can be rigorously estimated from samples. Our theory can be tighter than existing bounds and further generalizes to a broader tasks, losses, and stochastic labeling.

Distribution shift theory often serves as a theoretical framework for domain adaptation and domain generalization, where many algorithms have been developed (Sugiyama et al., 2007; Glorot et al., 2011; Sun and Saenko, 2016; Ganin et al., 2016; Pei et al., 2018; Arjovsky et al., 2019; Krueger et al., 2021; Rame et al., 2022). However, the DomainBed benchmark (Gulrajani and Lopez-Paz, 2020) shows that many algorithms do not outperform standard empirical risk minimization. This calls for tighter and more general theoretical frameworks to explain the generalization failures of these algorithms. In addition, the proposed γ∗\gamma^{*}-Y∣\midX shift takes a nested OT form, whose other mathematical properties have also been studied recently, such as the gradient flow of the Wasserstein-over-Wasserstein distance (Bonet et al., 2025).

Appendix B Technical Tools

In this section, we introduce several existing mathematical tools to prove the propositions in Appendix C.

B.1 Conditional Probability

Definition B.1 (Conditional Probability).

Let (Ω,ℱ,P)(\Omega,\mathcal{F},P) be a probability space and X:Ω→𝒳X:\Omega\to\mathcal{X} a random variable with distribution PXP_{X}. For event A∈ℱA\in\mathcal{F}, a PXP_{X}-measurable function P⁡(A∣X=x):𝒳→[0,1]P(A\mid X=x):\mathcal{X}\to[0,1] is the conditional probability of AA given XX if:

∀B∈ℬ𝒳,P(A∩{X∈B})=∫BP(A∣X=x)dPX(x)\forall B\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathcal{X}},\,P(A\cap\{X\in B\})=\int_{B}P(A\mid X=x)\,dP_{X}(x)

where ℬ𝒳\mathcal{B}_{\mathcal{X}} denotes the Borel σ\sigma-algebra on 𝒳\mathcal{X}.

The conditional probability is unique almost everywhere with respect to PXP_{X} (unique PXP_{X}-a.e.) (Kallenberg and Kallenberg, 1997). That is, for any PXP_{X}-null set ZZ with PX​(Z)=0P_{X}(Z)=0, ∫ZP⁡(A∣X=x)​d​PX​(x)=0\int_{Z}P(A\mid X=x)\,dP_{X}(x)=0, implying that P⁡(A∣X=x)P(A\mid X=x) can be assigned arbitrarily on ZZ without affecting its overall properties. Intuitively, it means discussing conditional probabilities on a null set is meaningless (Hájek, 2003).

B.2 McDiarmid’s Inequality

Lemma B.2 (McDiarmid’s Inequality).

Let Z1,…,ZnZ_{1},\ldots,Z_{n} be independent random variables taking values in sets 𝒵1,…,𝒵n\mathcal{Z}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{Z}_{n}, and let F:𝒵1×⋯×𝒵n→ℝF:\mathcal{Z}_{1}\times\cdots\times\mathcal{Z}_{n}\to\mathbb{R}. Assume FF satisfies the bounded-differences property: there exist constants c1,…,cn≥0c_{1},\ldots,c_{n}\geq 0 such that for every i∈[n]i\in[n] and any two inputs (z1,…,zn)(z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}) and (z1,…,zi′,…,zn)(z_{1},\ldots,z_{i}^{\prime},\ldots,z_{n}) differing only at the ii-th coordinate,

|F⁡(z1,…,zi,…,zn)−F⁡(z1,…,zi′,…,zn)|≤ci.\bigl|F(z_{1},\ldots,z_{i},\ldots,z_{n})-F(z_{1},\ldots,z_{i}^{\prime},\ldots,z_{n})\bigr|\;\leq\;c_{i}.

Then for any ε>0\varepsilon>0,

ℙ⁡(F⁡(Z1,…,Zn)−𝔼⁡[F⁡(Z1,…,Zn)]≥ε)≤exp⁡(−2​ε2∑i=1nci2),\mathbb{P}\Bigl(F(Z_{1},\ldots,Z_{n})-\mathbb{E}\bigl[F(Z_{1},\ldots,Z_{n})\bigr]\geq\varepsilon\Bigr)\;\leq\;\exp\!\left(-\frac{2\varepsilon^{2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_{i}^{2}}\right),

and

ℙ⁡(|F⁡(Z1,…,Zn)−𝔼⁡[F⁡(Z1,…,Zn)]|≥ε)≤ 2​exp⁡(−2​ε2∑i=1nci2).\mathbb{P}\Bigl(\bigl|F(Z_{1},\ldots,Z_{n})-\mathbb{E}[F(Z_{1},\ldots,Z_{n})]\bigr|\geq\varepsilon\Bigr)\;\leq\;2\exp\!\left(-\frac{2\varepsilon^{2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_{i}^{2}}\right).

B.3 Concentration for Empirical W1W_{1}

Lemma B.3 (Square-Exponential Moment Implies T1T_{1} (Bolley et al., 2007)).

Let (𝒳,ρ)(\mathcal{X},\rho) be a Polish metric space and μ\mu a Borel probability measure on 𝒳\mathcal{X}. Assume μ\mu admits a square-exponential moment: there exist a>0a>0 and x0∈𝒳x_{0}\in\mathcal{X} such that

∫𝒳exp⁡(a​ρ​(x,x0)2)​𝑑μ​(x)<∞.\int_{\mathcal{X}}\exp\!\bigl(a\,\rho(x,x_{0})^{2}\bigr)\,d\mu(x)<\infty.

Then μ\mu satisfies a T1​(λ)T_{1}(\lambda) transport-entropy inequality for some λ>0\lambda>0: for all probability measures ν\nu on 𝒳\mathcal{X},

W1​(μ,ν)≤2λ​H​(ν∣μ).W_{1}(\mu,\nu)\leq\sqrt{\frac{2}{\lambda}\,H(\nu\mid\mu)}.
Lemma B.4 (Bolley–Guillin Concentration for Empirical W1W_{1} (Bolley et al., 2007)).

Let μ\mu be a probability measure on (ℝd,∥⋅∥)(\mathbb{R}^{d},\|\cdot\|) that satisfies the transport inequality T1​(λ)T_{1}(\lambda) for some λ>0\lambda>0, namely for all probability measures ν\nu,

W1​(μ,ν)≤2λ​H​(ν∣μ),W_{1}(\mu,\nu)\;\leq\;\sqrt{\frac{2}{\lambda}\,H(\nu\mid\mu)},

where H⁡(ν∣μ)H(\nu\mid\mu) denotes the relative entropy. Let μ^=1N​∑i=1NδXi\hat{\mu}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\delta_{X_{i}} be the empirical measure of i.i.d. samples X1,…,XN∼μX_{1},\ldots,X_{N}\sim\mu. Then for any d′>dd^{\prime}>d and any λμ∈(0,λ)\lambda_{\mu}\in(0,\lambda), there exists a constant N0N_{0} depending only on λμ\lambda_{\mu}, d′d^{\prime}, and the squared-exponential moments of μ\mu such that for any ε>0\varepsilon>0 and any

N≥N0​max⁡(ε−(d′+2), 1),N\;\geq\;N_{0}\max\bigl(\varepsilon^{-(d^{\prime}+2)},\,1\bigr),

we have

ℙ⁡(W1​(μ,μ^)>ε)≤exp⁡(−λμ2​N​ε2).\mathbb{P}\bigl(W_{1}(\mu,\hat{\mu})>\varepsilon\bigr)\;\leq\;\exp\!\left(-\frac{\lambda_{\mu}}{2}\,N\,\varepsilon^{2}\right).

Appendix C Full proofs

C.1 Proof of Lemma 2.2

Proof.

Since supp⁡(PX′)∖supp⁡(PX)≠∅\operatorname{supp}(P_{X}^{\prime})\setminus\operatorname{supp}(P_{X})\neq\varnothing, pick x0∈supp⁡(PX′)∖supp⁡(PX)x_{0}\in\operatorname{supp}(P_{X}^{\prime})\setminus\operatorname{supp}(P_{X}). By Definition 2.1, x0∉supp⁡(PX)x_{0}\notin\operatorname{supp}(P_{X}) implies that there exists an open neighborhood U⊆𝒳U\subseteq\mathcal{X} with x0∈Ux_{0}\in U such that

PX​(U)=0.P_{X}(U)=0.

On the other hand, x0∈supp⁡(PX′)x_{0}\in\operatorname{supp}(P_{X}^{\prime}) implies PX′​(V)>0P_{X}^{\prime}(V)>0 for every open neighborhood V∋x0V\ni x_{0}, hence in particular PX′​(U)>0P_{X}^{\prime}(U)>0. Let Z:=UZ:=U. Then Z∈ℬ𝒳Z\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathcal{X}} and

PX​(Z)=0,PX′​(Z)>0.P_{X}(Z)=0,\qquad P_{X}^{\prime}(Z)>0.

Let P⁡(A∣X=x):𝒳→[0,1]P(A\mid X=x):\mathcal{X}\to[0,1] be a conditional probability in Definition B.1, i.e., for all B∈ℬ𝒳B\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathcal{X}},

P(A∩{X∈B})=∫BP(A∣X=x)dPX(x).P\bigl(A\cap\{X\in B\}\bigr)=\int_{B}P(A\mid X=x)\,dP_{X}(x).

For any constant c∈[0,1]c\in[0,1], define a modified function

P~​(A∣X=x):={P⁡(A∣X=x),x∉Z,c,x∈Z.\widetilde{P}(A\mid X=x):=\begin{cases}P(A\mid X=x),&x\notin Z,\\ c,&x\in Z.\end{cases}

For any B∈ℬ𝒳B\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathcal{X}},

∫BP~​(A∣X=x)​d​PX​(x)\displaystyle\int_{B}\widetilde{P}(A\mid X=x)\,dP_{X}(x) =∫B∖ZP⁡(A∣X=x)​d​PX​(x)+∫B∩Zc​d​PX​(x)\displaystyle=\int_{B\setminus Z}P(A\mid X=x)\,dP_{X}(x)+\int_{B\cap Z}c\,dP_{X}(x)
=∫B∖ZP⁡(A∣X=x)​d​PX​(x)+c​PX​(B∩Z)\displaystyle=\int_{B\setminus Z}P(A\mid X=x)\,dP_{X}(x)+c\,P_{X}(B\cap Z)
=∫B∖ZP(A∣X=x)dPX(x)(since PX(Z)=0)\displaystyle=\int_{B\setminus Z}P(A\mid X=x)\,dP_{X}(x)\qquad(\text{since }P_{X}(Z)=0)
=∫BP(A∣X=x)dPX(x)=P(A∩{X∈B}),\displaystyle=\int_{B}P(A\mid X=x)\,dP_{X}(x)=P\bigl(A\cap\{X\in B\}\bigr),

so P~​(A∣X=x)\widetilde{P}(A\mid X=x) is also a valid conditional probability of AA given XX by Definition B.1, as another version of P⁡(A∣X=x)P(A\mid X=x).

Now take expectation under PX′P_{X}^{\prime}:

𝔼PX′​[P~​(A∣X=x)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{P_{X}^{\prime}}[\,\widetilde{P}(A\mid X=x)\,] =∫𝒳P~​(A∣X=x)​d​PX′​(x)\displaystyle=\int_{\mathcal{X}}\widetilde{P}(A\mid X=x)\,dP_{X}^{\prime}(x)
=∫𝒳∖ZP⁡(A∣X=x)​d​PX′​(x)+∫Zc​d​PX′​(x)\displaystyle=\int_{\mathcal{X}\setminus Z}P(A\mid X=x)\,dP_{X}^{\prime}(x)+\int_{Z}c\,dP_{X}^{\prime}(x)
=∫𝒳∖ZP⁡(A∣X=x)​d​PX′​(x)+c​PX′​(Z).\displaystyle=\int_{\mathcal{X}\setminus Z}P(A\mid X=x)\,dP_{X}^{\prime}(x)+c\,P_{X}^{\prime}(Z).

Since PX′​(Z)>0P_{X}^{\prime}(Z)>0 and c∈[0,1]c\in[0,1] is arbitrary, the value of 𝔼PX′​[P⁡(A∣X=x)]\mathbb{E}_{P_{X}^{\prime}}[P(A\mid X=x)] can be changed by choosing different cc while preserving the defining property of conditional probability under PXP_{X}. Hence 𝔼PX′​[P⁡(A∣X=x)]\mathbb{E}_{P_{X}^{\prime}}[P(A\mid X=x)] is arbitrary. ∎

Remark

The above proof shows that support mismatch leads to arbitrariness. Broadly speaking, support mismatch commonly breaks the rigor of theoretical analyses. Some studies explicitly exclude it from analysis by extra assumptions, such as done in the absolute continuity in measure theory (Duncan, 1970), the positivity assumption in causal inference (Cole and Frangakis, 2009), or support overlap in importance sampling (Gelman and Meng, 1998).

C.2 Proof of Corollary 3.3

Proof.

By Definition 3.2,

SC​p​tγ∗=𝔼(xS,xT)∼γ∗​[W1​(𝒟Y|X=xSS,𝒟Y|X=xTT)].S_{Cpt}^{\gamma^{*}}=\mathbb{E}_{(x_{S},x_{T})\sim\gamma^{*}}\!\left[W_{1}\!\bigl(\mathcal{D}_{Y|X=x_{S}}^{S},\mathcal{D}_{Y|X=x_{T}}^{T}\bigr)\right].

Under deterministic labeling, 𝒟Y|X=xSS=δfS​(xS)\mathcal{D}_{Y|X=x_{S}}^{S}=\delta_{f_{S}(x_{S})} and 𝒟Y|X=xTT=δfT​(xT)\mathcal{D}_{Y|X=x_{T}}^{T}=\delta_{f_{T}(x_{T})}, hence

Sp​a​i​r​(xS,xT)=W1​(δfS​(xS),δfT​(xT)).S_{pair}(x_{S},x_{T})=W_{1}\!\bigl(\delta_{f_{S}(x_{S})},\delta_{f_{T}(x_{T})}\bigr).

For any a,b∈𝒴a,b\in\mathcal{Y}, any coupling π∈Γ⁡(δa,δb)\pi\in\Gamma(\delta_{a},\delta_{b}) must satisfy π⁡({a}×𝒴)=1\pi(\{a\}\times\mathcal{Y})=1 and π⁡(𝒴×{b})=1\pi(\mathcal{Y}\times\{b\})=1, hence π=δ(a,b)\pi=\delta_{(a,b)} is the unique coupling. Therefore,

W1​(δa,δb)=infπ∈Γ⁡(δa,δb)∫ρ𝒴​(y1,y2)​𝑑π=∫ρ𝒴​(y1,y2)​d​δ(a,b)​(y1,y2)=ρ𝒴​(a,b).W_{1}(\delta_{a},\delta_{b})=\inf_{\pi\in\Gamma(\delta_{a},\delta_{b})}\int\rho_{\mathcal{Y}}(y_{1},y_{2})\,d\pi=\int\rho_{\mathcal{Y}}(y_{1},y_{2})\,d\delta_{(a,b)}(y_{1},y_{2})=\rho_{\mathcal{Y}}(a,b).

Applying this with a=fS​(xS)a=f_{S}(x_{S}) and b=fT​(xT)b=f_{T}(x_{T}) yields Sp​a​i​r​(xS,xT)=ρ𝒴​(fS​(xS),fT​(xT))S_{pair}(x_{S},x_{T})=\rho_{\mathcal{Y}}(f_{S}(x_{S}),f_{T}(x_{T})), and thus

SC​p​tγ∗=𝔼(xS,xT)∼γ∗​[ρ𝒴​(fS​(xS),fT​(xT))],S_{Cpt}^{\gamma^{*}}=\mathbb{E}_{(x_{S},x_{T})\sim\gamma^{*}}\bigl[\rho_{\mathcal{Y}}(f_{S}(x_{S}),f_{T}(x_{T}))\bigr],

as claimed. ∎

C.3 Proof of Lemma 3.4

Proof.

Any γ∈Γ⁡(𝒟XS,𝒟XT)\gamma\in\Gamma(\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S},\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}) is a coupling of 𝒟XS\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S} and 𝒟XT\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}, hence its first marginal is 𝒟XS\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S} and its second marginal is 𝒟XT\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}.

Take any (xS,xT)∉supp⁡(𝒟XS)×supp⁡(𝒟XT)(x_{S},x_{T})\notin\operatorname{supp}(\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S})\times\operatorname{supp}(\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}). Then either xS∉supp⁡(𝒟XS)x_{S}\notin\operatorname{supp}(\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S}) or xT∉supp⁡(𝒟XT)x_{T}\notin\operatorname{supp}(\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}).

If xS∉supp⁡(𝒟XS)x_{S}\notin\operatorname{supp}(\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S}), by Definition 2.1 there exists an open neighborhood U⊆𝒳U\subseteq\mathcal{X} of xSx_{S} such that 𝒟XS​(U)=0\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S}(U)=0. Since the first marginal of γ\gamma is 𝒟XS\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S},

γ⁡(U×𝒳)=𝒟XS​(U)=0.\gamma(U\times\mathcal{X})=\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S}(U)=0.

In particular, for any open neighborhood VV of xTx_{T} we have γ⁡(U×V)≤γ⁡(U×𝒳)=0\gamma(U\times V)\leq\gamma(U\times\mathcal{X})=0, so γ⁡(U×V)=0\gamma(U\times V)=0. Thus, taking the product open set U×VU\times V containing (xS,xT)(x_{S},x_{T}), we conclude that (xS,xT)∉supp⁡(γ)(x_{S},x_{T})\notin\operatorname{supp}(\gamma) by Definition 2.1 applied on the product topology of 𝒳×𝒳\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X}.

The case xT∉supp⁡(𝒟XT)x_{T}\notin\operatorname{supp}(\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}) is symmetric: there exists an open V∋xTV\ni x_{T} with 𝒟XT​(V)=0\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}(V)=0, and using the second marginal of γ\gamma gives γ⁡(𝒳×V)=0\gamma(\mathcal{X}\times V)=0, hence γ⁡(U×V)=0\gamma(U\times V)=0 for any open U∋xSU\ni x_{S}, implying (xS,xT)∉supp⁡(γ)(x_{S},x_{T})\notin\operatorname{supp}(\gamma).

Therefore every point outside supp⁡(𝒟XS)×supp⁡(𝒟XT)\operatorname{supp}(\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S})\times\operatorname{supp}(\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}) is outside supp⁡(γ)\operatorname{supp}(\gamma), i.e.,

supp⁡(γ)⊆supp⁡(𝒟XS)×supp⁡(𝒟XT).\operatorname{supp}(\gamma)\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S})\times\operatorname{supp}(\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}).

∎

C.4 Proof of Lemma 3.5

Proof.

Let ν:=𝒟XS⊗𝒟XT\nu:=\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S}\otimes\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T} and consider the entropic optimal transport objective

J⁡(γ):=∫ρ𝒳​(xS,xT)​𝑑γ​(xS,xT)+β​H​(γ∣ν),γ∈Γ⁡(𝒟XS,𝒟XT).J(\gamma):=\int\rho_{\mathcal{X}}(x_{S},x_{T})\,d\gamma(x_{S},x_{T})+\beta\,H(\gamma\mid\nu),\qquad\gamma\in\Gamma(\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S},\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}).

We claim that JJ is strictly convex over the convex set Γ⁡(𝒟XS,𝒟XT)\Gamma(\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S},\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}). Indeed, the transport cost term γ↦∫ρ𝒳​𝑑γ\gamma\mapsto\int\rho_{\mathcal{X}}\,d\gamma is linear in γ\gamma. For the entropy term, write r=d​γd​νr=\frac{d\gamma}{d\nu}; then

H⁡(γ∣ν)=∫r​log⁡r​𝑑ν.H(\gamma\mid\nu)=\int r\log r\,d\nu.

For any γ1,γ2∈Γ⁡(𝒟XS,𝒟XT)\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2}\in\Gamma(\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S},\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}) with γ1≠γ2\gamma_{1}\neq\gamma_{2}, by Lemma 3.4,

supp⁡(γ1)⊆supp⁡(𝒟XS)×supp⁡(𝒟XT)=supp⁡(ν).\operatorname{supp}(\gamma_{1})\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S})\times\operatorname{supp}(\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T})=\operatorname{supp}(\nu).
supp⁡(γ2)⊆supp⁡(𝒟XS)×supp⁡(𝒟XT)=supp⁡(ν).\operatorname{supp}(\gamma_{2})\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S})\times\operatorname{supp}(\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T})=\operatorname{supp}(\nu).

Because φ⁡(t)=t​log⁡t\varphi(t)=t\log t is strictly convex on [0,∞)[0,\infty), for and any λ∈(0,1)\lambda\in(0,1),

H⁡(λ​γ1+(1−λ)​γ2∣ν)<λ​H​(γ1∣ν)+(1−λ)​H​(γ2∣ν),H\bigl(\lambda\gamma_{1}+(1-\lambda)\gamma_{2}\mid\nu\bigr)<\lambda H(\gamma_{1}\mid\nu)+(1-\lambda)H(\gamma_{2}\mid\nu),

hence (multiplying by β>0\beta>0) the whole objective satisfies

J⁡(λ​γ1+(1−λ)​γ2)<λ​J​(γ1)+(1−λ)​J​(γ2).J\bigl(\lambda\gamma_{1}+(1-\lambda)\gamma_{2}\bigr)<\lambda J(\gamma_{1})+(1-\lambda)J(\gamma_{2}).

Now suppose, toward a contradiction, that there are two distinct optimal couplings γ1≠γ2\gamma_{1}\neq\gamma_{2} minimizing JJ over Γ⁡(𝒟XS,𝒟XT)\Gamma(\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S},\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}). By convexity of Γ⁡(𝒟XS,𝒟XT)\Gamma(\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S},\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}), their mixture γλ:=λ​γ1+(1−λ)​γ2\gamma_{\lambda}:=\lambda\gamma_{1}+(1-\lambda)\gamma_{2} is feasible. Strict convexity then yields

J⁡(γλ)<λ​J​(γ1)+(1−λ)​J​(γ2)=infγ∈ΓJ⁡(γ),J(\gamma_{\lambda})<\lambda J(\gamma_{1})+(1-\lambda)J(\gamma_{2})=\inf_{\gamma\in\Gamma}J(\gamma),

a contradiction. Therefore the optimizer γ∗\gamma^{*} is unique. ∎

Proof.

infγ∈Γ⁡(𝒟XS,𝒟XT)∫ρ𝒳​(xS,xT)​𝑑γ​(xS,xT),\inf_{\gamma\in\Gamma(\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S},\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T})}\int\rho_{\mathcal{X}}(x_{S},x_{T})\,d\gamma(x_{S},x_{T}),

0=∫ρ𝒳​(xS,xT)​d​γ∗​(xS,xT).0=\int\rho_{\mathcal{X}}(x_{S},x_{T})\,d\gamma^{*}(x_{S},x_{T}).

Since the integrand is nonnegative, this implies ρ𝒳​(xS,xT)=0\rho_{\mathcal{X}}(x_{S},x_{T})=0 holds γ∗\gamma^{*}-almost surely, i.e., (xS,xT)∈ζ:={(x,x):x∈𝒳}(x_{S},x_{T})\in\zeta:=\{(x,x):x\in\mathcal{X}\} γ∗\gamma^{*}-a.s. Hence supp⁡(γ∗)⊆ζ\operatorname{supp}(\gamma^{*})\subseteq\zeta.

which proves γ∗=(Id,Id)#​𝒟XS\gamma^{*}=(\mathrm{Id},\mathrm{Id})_{\#}\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S} and the stated equivalent form. ∎

C.6 Proof of Theorem 3.7

Proof.

For β>0\beta>0, Lemma 3.5 ensures that the entropic optimal transport coupling γ∗\gamma^{*} in Definition 3.1 is unique. Hence any potential ambiguity of SC​p​tγ∗S_{Cpt}^{\gamma^{*}} can only come from the choice of versions of the conditional distributions.

Given any two versions of the source conditionals {𝒟Y|X=xS}x∈𝒳\{\mathcal{D}_{Y|X=x}^{S}\}_{x\in\mathcal{X}} and {𝒟~Y|X=xS}x∈𝒳\{\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}_{Y|X=x}^{S}\}_{x\in\mathcal{X}}, and any two versions of the target conditionals {𝒟Y|X=xT}x∈𝒳\{\mathcal{D}_{Y|X=x}^{T}\}_{x\in\mathcal{X}} and {𝒟~Y|X=xT}x∈𝒳\{\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}_{Y|X=x}^{T}\}_{x\in\mathcal{X}}, such that 𝒟Y|X=xS=𝒟~Y|X=xS\mathcal{D}_{Y|X=x}^{S}=\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}_{Y|X=x}^{S} holds 𝒟XS\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S}-a.e., and 𝒟Y|X=xT=𝒟~Y|X=xT\mathcal{D}_{Y|X=x}^{T}=\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}_{Y|X=x}^{T} holds 𝒟XT\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}-a.e. Therefore, there exist measurable sets ES,ET⊆𝒳E_{S},E_{T}\subseteq\mathcal{X} with 𝒟XS​(ES)=0\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S}(E_{S})=0 and 𝒟XT​(ET)=0\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}(E_{T})=0 such that the equalities hold for all x∉ESx\notin E_{S} and all x∉ETx\notin E_{T}, respectively.

Define the γ∗\gamma^{*}-Y||X shift under the two choices as

SC​p​tγ∗:=∫W1​(𝒟Y|X=xSS,𝒟Y|X=xTT)​d​γ∗​(xS,xT),S_{Cpt}^{\gamma^{*}}:=\int W_{1}\!\bigl(\mathcal{D}_{Y|X=x_{S}}^{S},\mathcal{D}_{Y|X=x_{T}}^{T}\bigr)\,d\gamma^{*}(x_{S},x_{T}),

C.13 Proof of Lemma 4.4

Proof.

We follow (Eckstein and Nutz, 2022). Recall that the entropically regularized OT problem is

Sentε(μ,ν,c):=infπ∈Π⁡(μ,ν)∫cdπ+εKL(π∥μ⊗ν),S^{\varepsilon}_{\mathrm{ent}}(\mu,\nu,c):=\inf_{\pi\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)}\int c\,d\pi+\varepsilon\,\mathrm{KL}(\pi\,\|\,\mu\otimes\nu),

has the same optimizer as

∫1βcdπ+KL(π∥μ⊗ν),\int\frac{1}{\beta}c\,d\pi+\mathrm{KL}(\pi\,\|\,\mu\otimes\nu),

Consider the product space 𝒳×𝒳\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X} with metric

ρ⁡((x1,x2),(x1′,x2′)):=ρ𝒳​(x1,x1′)+ρ𝒳​(x2,x2′).\rho\big((x_{1},x_{2}),(x_{1}^{\prime},x_{2}^{\prime})\big):=\rho_{\mathcal{X}}(x_{1},x_{1}^{\prime})+\rho_{\mathcal{X}}(x_{2},x_{2}^{\prime}).

|c⁡(x1,x2)−c⁡(x1′,x2′)|=|ρ𝒳​(x1,x2)−ρ𝒳​(x1′,x2′)|≤ρ𝒳​(x1,x1′)+ρ𝒳​(x2,x2′)=ρ⁡((x1,x2),(x1′,x2′)),\big|c(x_{1},x_{2})-c(x_{1}^{\prime},x_{2}^{\prime})\big|=\big|\rho_{\mathcal{X}}(x_{1},x_{2})-\rho_{\mathcal{X}}(x_{1}^{\prime},x_{2}^{\prime})\big|\leq\rho_{\mathcal{X}}(x_{1},x_{1}^{\prime})+\rho_{\mathcal{X}}(x_{2},x_{2}^{\prime})=\rho((x_{1},x_{2}),(x_{1}^{\prime},x_{2}^{\prime})),

|f⁡(xS,xT)−f⁡(xS,xT′)|≤M​LY|X​‖xT−xT′‖.\bigl|f(x_{S},x_{T})-f(x_{S},x_{T}^{\prime})\bigr|\leq ML_{Y|X}\|x_{T}-x_{T}^{\prime}\|.
