|f⁡(xS,xT)−f⁡(xS′,xT′)|≤M​LY|X​(‖xS−xS′‖+‖xT−xT′‖)=M​LY|X​ρ​((xS,xT),(xS′,xT′)).\bigl|f(x_{S},x_{T})-f(x_{S}^{\prime},x_{T}^{\prime})\bigr|\leq ML_{Y|X}\bigl(\|x_{S}-x_{S}^{\prime}\|+\|x_{T}-x_{T}^{\prime}\|\bigr)=ML_{Y|X}\,\rho\bigl((x_{S},x_{T}),(x_{S}^{\prime},x_{T}^{\prime})\bigr).

Thus ff is (M​LY|X)(ML_{Y|X})-Lipschitz on (ℝd×ℝd,ρ)(\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d},\rho).

Step 4.2: convert BB to a Wasserstein distance on couplings.

By the Kantorovich–Rubinstein duality for W1W_{1} on (ℝd×ℝd,ρ)(\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d},\rho), for any KK-Lipschitz function φ\varphi,

|𝔼π​[φ]−𝔼π′​[φ]|≤K​W1​(π,π′).\Bigl|\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[\varphi]-\mathbb{E}_{\pi^{\prime}}[\varphi]\Bigr|\leq K\,W_{1}(\pi,\pi^{\prime}).

Apply this with φ=f\varphi=f and K=M​LY|XK=ML_{Y|X}, π=γ¯∗\pi=\bar{\gamma}^{*}, π′=γ∗\pi^{\prime}=\gamma^{*}:

B=|𝔼γ¯∗​[f]−𝔼γ∗​[f]|≤M​LY|X​W1​(γ∗,γ¯∗).B=\bigl|\mathbb{E}_{\bar{\gamma}^{*}}[f]-\mathbb{E}_{\gamma^{*}}[f]\bigr|\leq ML_{Y|X}\,W_{1}(\gamma^{*},\bar{\gamma}^{*}).
Step 4.3: apply entropic OT stability and then concentration of marginals.

By Lemma 4.4,

W1​(γ∗,γ¯∗)≤Λ+2​2β​λγ∗​Λ,Λ:=W1​(μ,μ^)+W1​(ν,ν^).W_{1}(\gamma^{*},\bar{\gamma}^{*})\leq\varLambda+2\sqrt{\frac{2}{\beta\lambda_{\gamma^{*}}}}\sqrt{\varLambda},\qquad\varLambda:=W_{1}(\mu,\hat{\mu})+W_{1}(\nu,\hat{\nu}).

Therefore,

B≤M​LY|X​(Λ+2​2β​λγ∗​Λ).B\leq ML_{Y|X}\Bigl(\varLambda+2\sqrt{\frac{2}{\beta\lambda_{\gamma^{*}}}}\sqrt{\varLambda}\Bigr).

Fix ε2>0\varepsilon_{2}>0. If Λ≤2​ε2\varLambda\leq 2\varepsilon_{2}, then

Λ≤2​ε2,Λ+2​2β​λγ∗​Λ≤2​ε2+4​ε2β​λγ∗,\sqrt{\varLambda}\leq\sqrt{2\varepsilon_{2}},\qquad\varLambda+2\sqrt{\frac{2}{\beta\lambda_{\gamma^{*}}}}\sqrt{\varLambda}\leq 2\varepsilon_{2}+4\sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon_{2}}{\beta\lambda_{\gamma^{*}}}},

and hence

B≤2​M​LY|X​ε2+4​M​LY|X​ε2β​λγ∗.B\leq 2ML_{Y|X}\varepsilon_{2}+4ML_{Y|X}\sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon_{2}}{\beta\lambda_{\gamma^{*}}}}.

Consequently,

{B>2MLY|Xε2+4MLY|Xε2β​λγ∗}⊆{Λ>2ε2}.\Bigl\{B>2ML_{Y|X}\varepsilon_{2}+4ML_{Y|X}\sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon_{2}}{\beta\lambda_{\gamma^{*}}}}\Bigr\}\subseteq\{\varLambda>2\varepsilon_{2}\}.

By the union bound,

ℙ⁡(Λ>2​ε2)≤ℙ⁡(W1​(μ,μ^)>ε2)+ℙ⁡(W1​(ν,ν^)>ε2).\mathbb{P}(\varLambda>2\varepsilon_{2})\leq\mathbb{P}\bigl(W_{1}(\mu,\hat{\mu})>\varepsilon_{2}\bigr)+\mathbb{P}\bigl(W_{1}(\nu,\hat{\nu})>\varepsilon_{2}\bigr).

Since μ,ν\mu,\nu have finite squared-exponential moments on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, by Lemma B.3 and  B.4, there exist constants λS,λT>0\lambda_{S},\lambda_{T}>0 depending only on these moments such that for any ε2>0\varepsilon_{2}>0 there exists NN with, whenever NS,NT>NN_{S},N_{T}>N,

ℙ⁡(W1​(μ,μ^)>ε2)≤exp⁡(−λS​NS​ε222),ℙ⁡(W1​(ν,ν^)>ε2)≤exp⁡(−λT​NT​ε222).\mathbb{P}\bigl(W_{1}(\mu,\hat{\mu})>\varepsilon_{2}\bigr)\leq\exp\Bigl(-\frac{\lambda_{S}N_{S}\varepsilon_{2}^{2}}{2}\Bigr),\qquad\mathbb{P}\bigl(W_{1}(\nu,\hat{\nu})>\varepsilon_{2}\bigr)\leq\exp\Bigl(-\frac{\lambda_{T}N_{T}\varepsilon_{2}^{2}}{2}\Bigr).

Thus we conclude

ℙ⁡(B>2​M​LY|X​ε2+4​M​LY|X​ε2β​λγ∗)≤exp⁡(−λS​NS​ε222)+exp⁡(−λT​NT​ε222).\mathbb{P}\Bigl(B>2ML_{Y|X}\varepsilon_{2}+4ML_{Y|X}\sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon_{2}}{\beta\lambda_{\gamma^{*}}}}\Bigr)\leq\exp\Bigl(-\frac{\lambda_{S}N_{S}\varepsilon_{2}^{2}}{2}\Bigr)+\exp\Bigl(-\frac{\lambda_{T}N_{T}\varepsilon_{2}^{2}}{2}\Bigr).

Step 5: combine the two parts.

For any ε1,ε2>0\varepsilon_{1},\varepsilon_{2}>0, by the union bound,

ℙ⁡(|S^C​p​t−𝔼γ∗​[f]|>ε1+2​M​LY|X​ε2+4​M​LY|X​ε2β​λγ∗)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\Bigl(|\hat{S}_{Cpt}-\mathbb{E}_{\gamma^{*}}[f]|>\varepsilon_{1}+2ML_{Y|X}\varepsilon_{2}+4ML_{Y|X}\sqrt{\tfrac{\varepsilon_{2}}{\beta\lambda_{\gamma^{*}}}}\Bigr) ≤ℙ⁡(A>ε1)\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{P}(A>\varepsilon_{1})
+ℙ⁡(B>2​M​LY|X​ε2+4​M​LY|X​ε2β​λγ∗)\displaystyle\quad+\mathbb{P}\Bigl(B>2ML_{Y|X}\varepsilon_{2}+4ML_{Y|X}\sqrt{\tfrac{\varepsilon_{2}}{\beta\lambda_{\gamma^{*}}}}\Bigr)
≤2​exp⁡(−2​NS​NT​ε12(NS+NT)​M2)\displaystyle\leq 2\exp\Bigl(-\frac{2N_{S}N_{T}\,\varepsilon_{1}^{2}}{(N_{S}+N_{T})\,M^{2}}\Bigr)
+exp⁡(−λS​NS​ε222)+exp⁡(−λT​NT​ε222).\displaystyle\quad+\exp\Bigl(-\frac{\lambda_{S}N_{S}\varepsilon_{2}^{2}}{2}\Bigr)+\exp\Bigl(-\frac{\lambda_{T}N_{T}\varepsilon_{2}^{2}}{2}\Bigr).

Recalling 𝔼γ∗​[f]=SC​p​tγ∗+Δ\mathbb{E}_{\gamma^{*}}[f]=S_{Cpt}^{\gamma^{*}}+\varDelta, the left-hand side is exactly ℙ⁡(|S^C​p​t−SC​p​tγ∗−Δ|>⋯)\mathbb{P}(|\hat{S}_{Cpt}-S_{Cpt}^{\gamma^{*}}-\varDelta|>\cdots).

Step 6: parameter tying and the explicit Φ\varPhi.

Introduce a single auxiliary parameter ε0>0\varepsilon_{0}>0 and set

ε1:=Mε0,ε2:=λS−1/4λT−1/4ε0.\varepsilon_{1}:=M\varepsilon_{0},\qquad\varepsilon_{2}:=\lambda_{S}^{-1/4}\lambda_{T}^{-1/4}\,\varepsilon_{0}.

Then the three exponential terms become

2​exp⁡(−2​NS​NT​ε12(NS+NT)​M2)\displaystyle 2\exp\Bigl(-\frac{2N_{S}N_{T}\,\varepsilon_{1}^{2}}{(N_{S}+N_{T})\,M^{2}}\Bigr) =2​exp⁡(−2​NS​NT​ε02NS+NT),\displaystyle=2\exp\Bigl(-\frac{2N_{S}N_{T}\,\varepsilon_{0}^{2}}{N_{S}+N_{T}}\Bigr),
exp⁡(−λS​NS​ε222)\displaystyle\exp\Bigl(-\frac{\lambda_{S}N_{S}\varepsilon_{2}^{2}}{2}\Bigr) =exp⁡(−λS1/2​NS​ε022​λT1/2),\displaystyle=\exp\Bigl(-\frac{\lambda_{S}^{1/2}N_{S}\,\varepsilon_{0}^{2}}{2\lambda_{T}^{1/2}}\Bigr),
exp⁡(−λT​NT​ε222)\displaystyle\exp\Bigl(-\frac{\lambda_{T}N_{T}\varepsilon_{2}^{2}}{2}\Bigr) =exp⁡(−λT1/2​NT​ε022​λS1/2).\displaystyle=\exp\Bigl(-\frac{\lambda_{T}^{1/2}N_{T}\,\varepsilon_{0}^{2}}{2\lambda_{S}^{1/2}}\Bigr).

The deviation level on the left-hand side becomes

ε1+2​M​LY|X​ε2+4​M​LY|X​ε2β​λγ∗\displaystyle\varepsilon_{1}+2ML_{Y|X}\varepsilon_{2}+4ML_{Y|X}\sqrt{\tfrac{\varepsilon_{2}}{\beta\lambda_{\gamma^{*}}}} =Mε0+2MLY|XλS−1/4λT−1/4ε0+4MLY|Xβ−1/2λγ∗−1/2λS−1/8λT−1/8ε01/2.\displaystyle=M\varepsilon_{0}+2ML_{Y|X}\lambda_{S}^{-1/4}\lambda_{T}^{-1/4}\varepsilon_{0}+4ML_{Y|X}\beta^{-1/2}\lambda_{\gamma^{*}}^{-1/2}\lambda_{S}^{-1/8}\lambda_{T}^{-1/8}\varepsilon_{0}^{1/2}.

Define the constants

c2:=1+2LY|XλS−1/4λT−1/4,c1:=16LY|X2β−1λγ∗−1λS−1/4λT−1/4.c_{2}:=1+2L_{Y|X}\lambda_{S}^{-1/4}\lambda_{T}^{-1/4},\qquad c_{1}:=16L_{Y|X}^{2}\beta^{-1}\lambda_{\gamma^{*}}^{-1}\lambda_{S}^{-1/4}\lambda_{T}^{-1/4}.

Then the deviation level can be written compactly as

M⁡(c2​ε0+c1​ε0).M\Bigl(c_{2}\varepsilon_{0}+\sqrt{c_{1}\varepsilon_{0}}\Bigr).

Now choose ε0\varepsilon_{0} so that

M⁡(c2​ε0+c1​ε0)=ε.M\Bigl(c_{2}\varepsilon_{0}+\sqrt{c_{1}\varepsilon_{0}}\Bigr)=\varepsilon.

Let u:=ε0u:=\sqrt{\varepsilon_{0}}. The equation becomes c2​u2+c1​u=ε/Mc_{2}u^{2}+\sqrt{c_{1}}\,u=\varepsilon/M, whose positive solution is

u=c1+4​c2​(ε/M)−c12​c2,ε0=u2.u=\frac{\sqrt{c_{1}+4c_{2}(\varepsilon/M)}-\sqrt{c_{1}}}{2c_{2}},\qquad\varepsilon_{0}=u^{2}.

It is convenient to express ε02\varepsilon_{0}^{2} in the form ε02=Φ​ε22​M2\varepsilon_{0}^{2}=\frac{\varPhi\varepsilon^{2}}{2M^{2}}. Let

a:=c1​Mc2​ε(>0),Λ⁡(a):=a2+4​a+2−(a+2)​a2+4​a,Φ:=Λ⁡(a)c22.a:=\frac{c_{1}M}{c_{2}\varepsilon}\quad(>0),\qquad\varLambda(a):=a^{2}+4a+2-(a+2)\sqrt{a^{2}+4a},\qquad\varPhi:=\frac{\varLambda(a)}{c_{2}^{2}}.

A direct algebraic simplification (expanding (a+2−a2+4​a)2(a+2-\sqrt{a^{2}+4a})^{2}) shows

ε02=Φ​ε22​M2.\varepsilon_{0}^{2}=\frac{\varPhi\,\varepsilon^{2}}{2M^{2}}.

Substituting this ε02\varepsilon_{0}^{2} into the exponential terms yields

2​exp⁡(−2​NS​NT​ε02NS+NT)\displaystyle 2\exp\Bigl(-\frac{2N_{S}N_{T}\varepsilon_{0}^{2}}{N_{S}+N_{T}}\Bigr) =2​exp⁡(−NS​NT​Φ​ε2(NS+NT)​M2),\displaystyle=2\exp\Bigl(-\frac{N_{S}N_{T}\,\varPhi\,\varepsilon^{2}}{(N_{S}+N_{T})\,M^{2}}\Bigr),
exp⁡(−λS1/2​NS​ε022​λT1/2)\displaystyle\exp\Bigl(-\frac{\lambda_{S}^{1/2}N_{S}\varepsilon_{0}^{2}}{2\lambda_{T}^{1/2}}\Bigr) =exp⁡(−λS1/2​NS​Φ​ε24​λT1/2​M2),\displaystyle=\exp\Bigl(-\frac{\lambda_{S}^{1/2}N_{S}\,\varPhi\,\varepsilon^{2}}{4\lambda_{T}^{1/2}M^{2}}\Bigr),

C.15 Proof of Proposition 4.6

Proof.

Recall the notation used in the proof of Theorem 4.5: for (xS,xT)∈𝒳×𝒳(x_{S},x_{T})\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X} define

f⁡(xS,xT):=𝔼yS∼𝒟Y|X=xSS,yT∼𝒟Y|X=xTT​[ρ𝒴​(yS,yT)],Sp​a​i​r​(xS,xT):=W1​(𝒟Y|X=xSS,𝒟Y|X=xTT),f(x_{S},x_{T}):=\mathbb{E}_{y_{S}\sim\mathcal{D}_{Y|X=x_{S}}^{S},\,y_{T}\sim\mathcal{D}_{Y|X=x_{T}}^{T}}\bigl[\rho_{\mathcal{Y}}(y_{S},y_{T})\bigr],\qquad S_{pair}(x_{S},x_{T}):=W_{1}\!\bigl(\mathcal{D}_{Y|X=x_{S}}^{S},\mathcal{D}_{Y|X=x_{T}}^{T}\bigr),

and the bias is

Δ=𝔼(xS,xT)∼γ∗​[f⁡(xS,xT)−Sp​a​i​r​(xS,xT)].\varDelta=\mathbb{E}_{(x_{S},x_{T})\sim\gamma^{*}}\!\bigl[f(x_{S},x_{T})-S_{pair}(x_{S},x_{T})\bigr].

Under deterministic labeling, 𝒟Y|X=xSS=δfS​(xS)\mathcal{D}_{Y|X=x_{S}}^{S}=\delta_{f_{S}(x_{S})} and 𝒟Y|X=xTT=δfT​(xT)\mathcal{D}_{Y|X=x_{T}}^{T}=\delta_{f_{T}(x_{T})}. Hence the random variables yS,yTy_{S},y_{T} are almost surely equal to fS​(xS),fT​(xT)f_{S}(x_{S}),f_{T}(x_{T}), and thus

f⁡(xS,xT)=𝔼⁡[ρ𝒴​(yS,yT)]=ρ𝒴​(fS​(xS),fT​(xT)).f(x_{S},x_{T})=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\rho_{\mathcal{Y}}(y_{S},y_{T})\bigr]=\rho_{\mathcal{Y}}\bigl(f_{S}(x_{S}),f_{T}(x_{T})\bigr).

On the other hand, the Wasserstein-11 distance between two Dirac measures is exactly the ground metric:

Sp​a​i​r​(xS,xT)=W1​(δfS​(xS),δfT​(xT))=ρ𝒴​(fS​(xS),fT​(xT)).S_{pair}(x_{S},x_{T})=W_{1}\!\bigl(\delta_{f_{S}(x_{S})},\delta_{f_{T}(x_{T})}\bigr)=\rho_{\mathcal{Y}}\bigl(f_{S}(x_{S}),f_{T}(x_{T})\bigr).

Therefore f⁡(xS,xT)−Sp​a​i​r​(xS,xT)=0f(x_{S},x_{T})-S_{pair}(x_{S},x_{T})=0 for all (xS,xT)(x_{S},x_{T}), and so

Δ=𝔼γ∗​[f⁡(xS,xT)−Sp​a​i​r​(xS,xT)]=0.\varDelta=\mathbb{E}_{\gamma^{*}}\!\bigl[f(x_{S},x_{T})-S_{pair}(x_{S},x_{T})\bigr]=0.

This concludes the proof. ∎

C.16 Proof of Proposition 4.7

Proof.

We follow the notation used in the proof of Theorem 4.5. For (xS,xT)∈𝒳×𝒳(x_{S},x_{T})\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X}, define

f⁡(xS,xT):=𝔼yS∼𝒟Y|X=xSS,yT∼𝒟Y|X=xTT​[‖yS−yT‖],Sp​a​i​r​(xS,xT):=W1​(𝒟Y|X=xSS,𝒟Y|X=xTT),f(x_{S},x_{T}):=\mathbb{E}_{y_{S}\sim\mathcal{D}_{Y|X=x_{S}}^{S},\;y_{T}\sim\mathcal{D}_{Y|X=x_{T}}^{T}}\bigl[\|y_{S}-y_{T}\|\bigr],\qquad S_{pair}(x_{S},x_{T}):=W_{1}\!\bigl(\mathcal{D}_{Y|X=x_{S}}^{S},\mathcal{D}_{Y|X=x_{T}}^{T}\bigr),

and recall that

Δ=𝔼(xS,xT)∼γ∗​[f⁡(xS,xT)−Sp​a​i​r​(xS,xT)].\varDelta=\mathbb{E}_{(x_{S},x_{T})\sim\gamma^{*}}\bigl[f(x_{S},x_{T})-S_{pair}(x_{S},x_{T})\bigr].

Lower bound Δ≥0\varDelta\geq 0.

For each fixed (xS,xT)(x_{S},x_{T}), the product measure 𝒟Y|X=xSS⊗𝒟Y|X=xTT\mathcal{D}_{Y|X=x_{S}}^{S}\otimes\mathcal{D}_{Y|X=x_{T}}^{T} belongs to Γ⁡(𝒟Y|X=xSS,𝒟Y|X=xTT)\Gamma\!\bigl(\mathcal{D}_{Y|X=x_{S}}^{S},\mathcal{D}_{Y|X=x_{T}}^{T}\bigr). Since Sp​a​i​r​(xS,xT)S_{pair}(x_{S},x_{T}) is the infimum of 𝔼⁡[‖yS−yT‖]\mathbb{E}[\|y_{S}-y_{T}\|] over all such couplings,

Sp​a​i​r​(xS,xT)≤𝔼𝒟Y|X=xSS⊗𝒟Y|X=xTT​[‖yS−yT‖]=f⁡(xS,xT).S_{pair}(x_{S},x_{T})\leq\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}_{Y|X=x_{S}}^{S}\otimes\mathcal{D}_{Y|X=x_{T}}^{T}}\bigl[\|y_{S}-y_{T}\|\bigr]=f(x_{S},x_{T}).

Thus f⁡(xS,xT)−Sp​a​i​r​(xS,xT)≥0f(x_{S},x_{T})-S_{pair}(x_{S},x_{T})\geq 0 pointwise, hence Δ≥0\varDelta\geq 0.

An upper bound for each pair (xS,xT)(x_{S},x_{T}).

Fix (xS,xT)(x_{S},x_{T}) and write P:=𝒟Y|X=xSSP:=\mathcal{D}_{Y|X=x_{S}}^{S} and Q:=𝒟Y|X=xTTQ:=\mathcal{D}_{Y|X=x_{T}}^{T}. Let their means be

mS​(xS):=𝔼y∼P​[y],mT​(xT):=𝔼y∼Q​[y],m_{S}(x_{S}):=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim P}[y],\qquad m_{T}(x_{T}):=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim Q}[y],

For independent draws yS∼Py_{S}\sim P and yT∼Qy_{T}\sim Q, the triangle inequality yields

‖yS−yT‖≤‖yS−mS​(xS)‖+‖mS​(xS)−mT​(xT)‖+‖mT​(xT)−yT‖.\|y_{S}-y_{T}\|\leq\|y_{S}-m_{S}(x_{S})\|+\|m_{S}(x_{S})-m_{T}(x_{T})\|+\|m_{T}(x_{T})-y_{T}\|.

Taking expectation gives

f⁡(xS,xT)≤𝔼y∼P​[‖y−mS​(xS)‖]+‖mS​(xS)−mT​(xT)‖+𝔼y∼Q​[‖y−mT​(xT)‖].f(x_{S},x_{T})\leq\mathbb{E}_{y\sim P}\bigl[\|y-m_{S}(x_{S})\|\bigr]+\|m_{S}(x_{S})-m_{T}(x_{T})\|+\mathbb{E}_{y\sim Q}\bigl[\|y-m_{T}(x_{T})\|\bigr].

Next we lower bound Sp​a​i​r​(xS,xT)=W1​(P,Q)S_{pair}(x_{S},x_{T})=W_{1}(P,Q) by the distance between the means. Let π∈Γ⁡(P,Q)\pi\in\Gamma(P,Q) be any coupling, and denote mP:=𝔼y∼P​[y]m_{P}:=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim P}[y], mQ:=𝔼y∼Q​[y]m_{Q}:=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim Q}[y]. Since ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| is convex, Jensen’s inequality yields

𝔼(y,y′)∼π​[‖y−y′‖]≥‖𝔼(y,y′)∼π​[y−y′]‖.\mathbb{E}_{(y,y^{\prime})\sim\pi}\bigl[\|y-y^{\prime}\|\bigr]\;\geq\;\Bigl\|\mathbb{E}_{(y,y^{\prime})\sim\pi}[\,y-y^{\prime}\,]\Bigr\|.

By the marginal constraints of π\pi, we have 𝔼(y,y′)∼π​[y]=mP\mathbb{E}_{(y,y^{\prime})\sim\pi}[y]=m_{P} and 𝔼(y,y′)∼π​[y′]=mQ\mathbb{E}_{(y,y^{\prime})\sim\pi}[y^{\prime}]=m_{Q}, hence

‖𝔼(y,y′)∼π​[y−y′]‖=‖mP−mQ‖.\Bigl\|\mathbb{E}_{(y,y^{\prime})\sim\pi}[\,y-y^{\prime}\,]\Bigr\|=\|m_{P}-m_{Q}\|.

Therefore, for every π∈Γ⁡(P,Q)\pi\in\Gamma(P,Q),

𝔼(y,y′)∼π​[‖y−y′‖]≥‖mP−mQ‖.\mathbb{E}_{(y,y^{\prime})\sim\pi}\bigl[\|y-y^{\prime}\|\bigr]\;\geq\;\|m_{P}-m_{Q}\|.

Taking the infimum over π∈Γ⁡(P,Q)\pi\in\Gamma(P,Q) gives

W1​(P,Q)=infπ∈Γ⁡(P,Q)𝔼(y,y′)∼π​[‖y−y′‖]≥‖mP−mQ‖.W_{1}(P,Q)=\inf_{\pi\in\Gamma(P,Q)}\mathbb{E}_{(y,y^{\prime})\sim\pi}\bigl[\|y-y^{\prime}\|\bigr]\;\geq\;\|m_{P}-m_{Q}\|.

Combining the two displays and canceling the middle term yields

f⁡(xS,xT)−Sp​a​i​r​(xS,xT)≤𝔼y∼P​[‖y−mS​(xS)‖]+𝔼y∼Q​[‖y−mT​(xT)‖].f(x_{S},x_{T})-S_{pair}(x_{S},x_{T})\leq\mathbb{E}_{y\sim P}\bigl[\|y-m_{S}(x_{S})\|\bigr]+\mathbb{E}_{y\sim Q}\bigl[\|y-m_{T}(x_{T})\|\bigr].

Integrate over γ∗\gamma^{*} and relate to irreducible errors.

Taking expectation over (xS,xT)∼γ∗(x_{S},x_{T})\sim\gamma^{*} and using that the marginals of γ∗\gamma^{*} are 𝒟XS\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S} and 𝒟XT\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T},

Δ≤𝔼x∼𝒟XS​[𝔼⁡[‖Y(S)−mS​(x)‖∣X(S)=x]]+𝔼x∼𝒟XT​[𝔼⁡[‖Y(T)−mT​(x)‖∣X(T)=x]].\varDelta\leq\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S}}\Bigl[\mathbb{E}\bigl[\|Y^{(S)}-m_{S}(x)\|\mid X^{(S)}=x\bigr]\Bigr]+\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}}\Bigl[\mathbb{E}\bigl[\|Y^{(T)}-m_{T}(x)\|\mid X^{(T)}=x\bigr]\Bigr].

For any random variable Z≥0Z\geq 0, 𝔼⁡[Z]≤𝔼⁡[Z2]\mathbb{E}[Z]\leq\sqrt{\mathbb{E}[Z^{2}]}, hence

𝔼⁡[‖Y(S)−mS​(x)‖∣X(S)=x]≤𝔼⁡[‖Y(S)−mS​(x)‖2∣X(S)=x],\mathbb{E}\bigl[\|Y^{(S)}-m_{S}(x)\|\mid X^{(S)}=x\bigr]\leq\sqrt{\mathbb{E}\bigl[\|Y^{(S)}-m_{S}(x)\|^{2}\mid X^{(S)}=x\bigr]},

and similarly for the target term. Thus

Δ≤𝔼x∼𝒟XS​[𝔼⁡[‖Y(S)−mS​(x)‖2∣X(S)=x]]+𝔼x∼𝒟XT​[𝔼⁡[‖Y(T)−mT​(x)‖2∣X(T)=x]].\varDelta\leq\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S}}\Bigl[\sqrt{\mathbb{E}\bigl[\|Y^{(S)}-m_{S}(x)\|^{2}\mid X^{(S)}=x\bigr]}\Bigr]+\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}}\Bigl[\sqrt{\mathbb{E}\bigl[\|Y^{(T)}-m_{T}(x)\|^{2}\mid X^{(T)}=x\bigr]}\Bigr].

Since ⋅\sqrt{\cdot} is concave on ℝ+\mathbb{R}_{+}, Jensen’s inequality gives

𝔼x∼𝒟XS​[𝔼⁡[‖Y(S)−mS​(x)‖2∣X(S)=x]]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}_{X}^{S}}\Bigl[\sqrt{\mathbb{E}\bigl[\|Y^{(S)}-m_{S}(x)\|^{2}\mid X^{(S)}=x\bigr]}\Bigr] ≤𝔼(x,y)∼𝒟X​YS​[‖y−mS​(x)‖2],\displaystyle\leq\sqrt{\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}_{XY}^{S}}\bigl[\|y-m_{S}(x)\|^{2}\bigr]},
𝔼x∼𝒟XT​[𝔼⁡[‖Y(T)−mT​(x)‖2∣X(T)=x]]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}_{X}^{T}}\Bigl[\sqrt{\mathbb{E}\bigl[\|Y^{(T)}-m_{T}(x)\|^{2}\mid X^{(T)}=x\bigr]}\Bigr] ≤𝔼(x,y)∼𝒟X​YT​[‖y−mT​(x)‖2].\displaystyle\leq\sqrt{\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}_{XY}^{T}}\bigl[\|y-m_{T}(x)\|^{2}\bigr]}.

Finally, under squared loss on ℝd′\mathbb{R}^{d^{\prime}}, the minimizer of 𝔼⁡[‖Y−g⁡(x)‖2∣X=x]\mathbb{E}[\|Y-g(x)\|^{2}\!\mid\!X=x] is g⁡(x)=𝔼⁡[Y∣X=x]g(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y\!\mid\!X=x]. Therefore the functions mS​(x)=𝔼⁡[Y(S)∣X(S)=x]m_{S}(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y^{(S)}\!\mid\!X^{(S)}=x] and mT​(x)=𝔼⁡[Y(T)∣X(T)=x]m_{T}(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y^{(T)}\!\mid\!X^{(T)}=x] achieve the infima of I⁡(𝒟X​YS)\mathrm{I}(\mathcal{D}_{XY}^{S}) and I⁡(𝒟X​YT)\mathrm{I}(\mathcal{D}_{XY}^{T}), i.e.,

𝔼(x,y)∼𝒟X​YS​[‖y−mS​(x)‖2]=I⁡(𝒟X​YS),𝔼(x,y)∼𝒟X​YT​[‖y−mT​(x)‖2]=I⁡(𝒟X​YT).\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}_{XY}^{S}}\bigl[\|y-m_{S}(x)\|^{2}\bigr]=\mathrm{I}(\mathcal{D}_{XY}^{S}),\qquad\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}_{XY}^{T}}\bigl[\|y-m_{T}(x)\|^{2}\bigr]=\mathrm{I}(\mathcal{D}_{XY}^{T}).

Putting the above bounds together yields

Δ≤I⁡(𝒟X​YS)+I⁡(𝒟X​YT),\varDelta\leq\sqrt{\mathrm{I}(\mathcal{D}_{XY}^{S})}+\sqrt{\mathrm{I}(\mathcal{D}_{XY}^{T})},

which completes the proof. ∎

Appendix D Analysis of Lipschitz Constants: Results and Proofs

D.1 Lipschitz Constant of the Sigmoid Function

Proposition D.1 (Lipschitz constant of the sigmoid).

Let σ:ℝ→ℝ\sigma:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} be the sigmoid function

σ⁡(x)=11+e−x.\sigma(x)\;=\;\frac{1}{1+e^{-x}}.

Then σ\sigma is globally 14\frac{1}{4}-Lipschitz on ℝ\mathbb{R}.

Proof.

We first compute the derivative:

σ′​(x)=dd​x​(1+e−x)−1=e−x(1+e−x)2.\sigma^{\prime}(x)=\frac{d}{dx}\Bigl(1+e^{-x}\Bigr)^{-1}=\frac{e^{-x}}{\bigl(1+e^{-x}\bigr)^{2}}.

Using σ⁡(x)=11+e−x\sigma(x)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-x}} and 1−σ⁡(x)=e−x1+e−x1-\sigma(x)=\frac{e^{-x}}{1+e^{-x}}, we can rewrite

σ′​(x)=σ⁡(x)​(1−σ⁡(x)).\sigma^{\prime}(x)=\sigma(x)\bigl(1-\sigma(x)\bigr).

Let u=σ⁡(x)∈(0,1)u=\sigma(x)\in(0,1). Then σ′​(x)=u⁡(1−u)\sigma^{\prime}(x)=u(1-u), and for all u∈[0,1]u\in[0,1],

u⁡(1−u)=u−u2≤maxt∈[0,1]⁡(t−t2)=14,u(1-u)=u-u^{2}\;\leq\;\max_{t\in[0,1]}(t-t^{2})=\frac{1}{4},

where the maximum is attained at t=12t=\frac{1}{2}. Hence 0<σ′​(x)≤140<\sigma^{\prime}(x)\leq\frac{1}{4} for all xx.

Now fix any x,y∈ℝx,y\in\mathbb{R}. Since σ\sigma is differentiable on ℝ\mathbb{R} (hence continuous), by the mean value theorem, there exists cc between xx and yy such that

σ⁡(x)−σ⁡(y)=σ′​(c)​(x−y).\sigma(x)-\sigma(y)=\sigma^{\prime}(c)\,(x-y).

Taking absolute values and using σ′​(c)≤14\sigma^{\prime}(c)\leq\frac{1}{4} yields

|σ⁡(x)−σ⁡(y)|=|σ′​(c)|​|x−y|≤14​|x−y|,|\sigma(x)-\sigma(y)|=|\sigma^{\prime}(c)|\,|x-y|\leq\frac{1}{4}|x-y|,

so σ\sigma is 14\frac{1}{4}-Lipschitz. ∎

D.2 Lipschitz Constant of the Logistic Regression

Proposition D.2 (Lipschitz constant of logistic regression under ℓp\ell_{p}/ℓq\ell_{q}).

Fix w∈ℝdw\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and b∈ℝb\in\mathbb{R}. Define

hw,b​(x)=σ⁡(w⊤​x+b),σ⁡(t)=11+e−t.h_{w,b}(x)\;=\;\sigma\!\bigl(w^{\top}x+b\bigr),\qquad\sigma(t)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-t}}.

Let p∈[1,∞]p\in[1,\infty] and let q∈[1,∞]q\in[1,\infty] be its Hölder conjugate, i.e., 1p+1q=1\frac{1}{p}+\frac{1}{q}=1. Then hw,bh_{w,b} is globally ‖w‖q4\frac{\|w\|_{q}}{4}-Lipschitz with respect to ∥⋅∥p\|\cdot\|_{p}, namely for all x,x′∈ℝdx,x^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{d},

|hw,b​(x)−hw,b​(x′)|≤‖w‖q4​‖x−x′‖p.\bigl|h_{w,b}(x)-h_{w,b}(x^{\prime})\bigr|\;\leq\;\frac{\|w\|_{q}}{4}\,\|x-x^{\prime}\|_{p}.

In particular, under ∥⋅∥2\|\cdot\|_{2}, the Lipschitz constant equals ‖w‖2/4\|w\|_{2}/4.

Proof.

For any x,x′∈ℝdx,x^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, apply the mean value theorem to σ\sigma to obtain some ξ\xi between w⊤​x+bw^{\top}x+b and w⊤​x′+bw^{\top}x^{\prime}+b such that

hw,b​(x)−hw,b​(x′)=σ′​(ξ)​w⊤​(x−x′).h_{w,b}(x)-h_{w,b}(x^{\prime})=\sigma^{\prime}(\xi)\,w^{\top}(x-x^{\prime}).

Thus

|hw,b​(x)−hw,b​(x′)|≤|σ′​(ξ)|​|w⊤​(x−x′)|.\bigl|h_{w,b}(x)-h_{w,b}(x^{\prime})\bigr|\leq|\sigma^{\prime}(\xi)|\,\bigl|w^{\top}(x-x^{\prime})\bigr|.

By Proposition D.1, we have |σ′​(ξ)|≤14|\sigma^{\prime}(\xi)|\leq\frac{1}{4}. By Hölder’s inequality with conjugate exponents (p,q)(p,q),

|w⊤​(x−x′)|≤‖w‖q​‖x−x′‖p.\bigl|w^{\top}(x-x^{\prime})\bigr|\leq\|w\|_{q}\,\|x-x^{\prime}\|_{p}.

Combining the two inequalities yields

|hw,b​(x)−hw,b​(x′)|≤14​‖w‖q​‖x−x′‖p,\bigl|h_{w,b}(x)-h_{w,b}(x^{\prime})\bigr|\leq\frac{1}{4}\,\|w\|_{q}\,\|x-x^{\prime}\|_{p},

which proves the claim. ∎

D.3 Lipschitz Constant of the Linear Multi-class Classifier

Proposition D.3.1 (Lipschitz constant of the linear classifier under ∥⋅∥2\|\cdot\|_{2}).

Let W∈ℝN×dW\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d} and b∈ℝNb\in\mathbb{R}^{N}. Define

f⁡(x)=softmax⁡(W​x+b)∈ΔN−1,x∈ℝd.f(x)=\mathrm{softmax}(Wx+b)\in\Delta^{N-1},\qquad x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.

Here ΔN−1:={p∈ℝN:pi≥0,∀i,∑i=1Npi=1}\Delta^{N-1}:=\{p\in\mathbb{R}^{N}:\ p_{i}\geq 0,\ \forall i,\ \sum_{i=1}^{N}p_{i}=1\} denotes the probability simplex. Let wi⊤w_{i}^{\top} denote the ii-th row of WW and define

D⁡(W):=maxi,j∈[N]⁡‖wi−wj‖2.D(W):=\max_{i,j\in[N]}\|w_{i}-w_{j}\|_{2}.

Then ff is Lipschitz from (ℝd,∥⋅∥2)(\mathbb{R}^{d},\|\cdot\|_{2}) to (ℝN,∥⋅∥2)(\mathbb{R}^{N},\|\cdot\|_{2}) and its optimal Lipschitz constant equals

supx∈ℝd‖∇f​(x)‖2=12​2​D​(W),\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}\|\nabla f(x)\|_{2}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\,D(W),

where ∥⋅∥2\|\cdot\|_{2} denotes the matrix operator norm induced by the vector ∥⋅∥2\|\cdot\|_{2} norm.

Proof.

For z∈ℝNz\in\mathbb{R}^{N}, write p=softmax⁡(z)∈ΔN−1p=\mathrm{softmax}(z)\in\Delta^{N-1}. The Jacobian of softmax is

J⁡(p)=∇zsoftmax​(z)=Diag⁡(p)−p​p⊤,J(p)=\nabla_{z}\,\mathrm{softmax}(z)=\mathrm{Diag}(p)-pp^{\top},

where Diag⁡(p)\mathrm{Diag}(p) is the diagonal matrix with diagonal entries p1,…,pNp_{1},\dots,p_{N}. By the chain rule, for p=softmax⁡(W​x+b)p=\mathrm{softmax}(Wx+b),

∇f​(x)=J​(p)​W.\nabla f(x)=J(p)\,W.

Therefore,

supx∈ℝd‖∇f​(x)‖2=supp∈ΔN−1‖J⁡(p)​W‖2.\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}\|\nabla f(x)\|_{2}=\sup_{p\in\Delta^{N-1}}\|J(p)W\|_{2}. (16)

Fix p∈ΔN−1p\in\Delta^{N-1} and a unit vector u∈ℝdu\in\mathbb{R}^{d} with ‖u‖2=1\|u\|_{2}=1. Let

v:=W​u∈ℝN,μ:=p⊤​v.v:=Wu\in\mathbb{R}^{N},\qquad\mu:=p^{\top}v.

and μ\mu represents the mean of vv under the probability distribution pp. We have

J⁡(p)​v=(Diag⁡(p)−p​p⊤)​v=Diag⁡(p)​(v−μ​𝟏),J(p)v=\bigl(\mathrm{Diag}(p)-pp^{\top}\bigr)v=\mathrm{Diag}(p)\bigl(v-\mu\mathbf{1}\bigr),

hence

‖J⁡(p)​W​u‖22=‖J⁡(p)​v‖22=∑i=1Npi2​(vi−μ)2.\|J(p)Wu\|_{2}^{2}=\|J(p)v\|_{2}^{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}p_{i}^{2}\,(v_{i}-\mu)^{2}. (17)

Now fix v∈ℝNv\in\mathbb{R}^{N} and consider the quantity

Φ⁡(v):=supp∈ΔN−1∑i=1Npi2​(vi−p⊤​v)2.\Phi(v):=\sup_{p\in\Delta^{N-1}}\sum_{i=1}^{N}p_{i}^{2}\,(v_{i}-p^{\top}v)^{2}.

Indeed, for any p∈ΔN−1p\in\Delta^{N-1},

∑i=1Npi2​(vi−μ)2≤(maxi⁡pi)​∑i=1Npi​(vi−μ)2=(maxi⁡pi)​Varp​(v),\sum_{i=1}^{N}p_{i}^{2}(v_{i}-\mu)^{2}\leq\Big(\max_{i}p_{i}\Big)\sum_{i=1}^{N}p_{i}(v_{i}-\mu)^{2}=\Big(\max_{i}p_{i}\Big)\mathrm{Var}_{p}(v),

where Varp​(v):=∑ipi​(vi−μ)2\mathrm{Var}_{p}(v):=\sum_{i}p_{i}(v_{i}-\mu)^{2}, which represents the variance of vv under the probability distribution pp. If pp is supported on two values m:=mini⁡vim:=\min_{i}v_{i} and M:=maxi⁡viM:=\max_{i}v_{i} with masses α\alpha and 1−α1-\alpha, let r:=M−mr:=M-m, then

∑i=1Npi2​(vi−μ)2=2​α2​(1−α)2​r2≤r28,\sum_{i=1}^{N}p_{i}^{2}(v_{i}-\mu)^{2}=2\alpha^{2}(1-\alpha)^{2}r^{2}\leq\frac{r^{2}}{8},

with equality at α=12\alpha=\tfrac{1}{2}. Since any mass placed at intermediate values of vv cannot increase the range-based extremum, we obtain Φ⁡(v)=r2/8\Phi(v)=r^{2}/8, and the optimal pp is supported on indices attaining MM and mm.

Combining (17), for any unit uu,

supp∈ΔN−1‖J⁡(p)​W​u‖2=12​2​(maxi⁡(W​u)i−minj⁡(W​u)j).\sup_{p\in\Delta^{N-1}}\|J(p)Wu\|_{2}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\Big(\max_{i}(Wu)_{i}-\min_{j}(Wu)_{j}\Big). (18)

Finally, maximize the range over uu. Writing (W​u)i=wi⊤​u(Wu)_{i}=w_{i}^{\top}u, we have

maxi⁡(W​u)i−minj⁡(W​u)j=maxi,j⁡(wi−wj)⊤​u.\max_{i}(Wu)_{i}-\min_{j}(Wu)_{j}=\max_{i,j}(w_{i}-w_{j})^{\top}u.

Thus,

sup‖u‖2=1(maxi⁡(W​u)i−minj⁡(W​u)j)=max⁡sup‖u‖2=1i,j⁡(wi−wj)⊤​u=maxi,j⁡‖wi−wj‖2=D⁡(W).\sup_{\|u\|_{2}=1}\Big(\max_{i}(Wu)_{i}-\min_{j}(Wu)_{j}\Big)=\max_{i,j}\sup_{\|u\|_{2}=1}(w_{i}-w_{j})^{\top}u=\max_{i,j}\|w_{i}-w_{j}\|_{2}=D(W).

Plugging this into (18) and then into (16) yields

supx∈ℝd‖∇f​(x)‖2\displaystyle\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}\|\nabla f(x)\|_{2}
=\displaystyle= supp∈ΔN−1‖J⁡(p)​W‖2\displaystyle\sup_{p\in\Delta^{N-1}}\|J(p)W\|_{2}
=\displaystyle= supp∈ΔN−1sup‖u‖2=1‖J⁡(p)​W​u‖2\displaystyle\sup_{p\in\Delta^{N-1}}\sup_{\|u\|_{2}=1}\|J(p)Wu\|_{2}
=\displaystyle= sup‖u‖2=1supp∈ΔN−1‖J⁡(p)​W​u‖2\displaystyle\sup_{\|u\|_{2}=1}\sup_{p\in\Delta^{N-1}}\|J(p)Wu\|_{2}
=\displaystyle= 12​2​D​(W)\displaystyle\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\,D(W)

Proposition D.3.2 (Lipschitz constant of the linear classifier under ∥⋅∥2→∥⋅∥1\|\cdot\|_{2}\to\|\cdot\|_{1}).

Let W∈ℝN×dW\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d} and b∈ℝNb\in\mathbb{R}^{N}. Define

f⁡(x)=softmax⁡(W​x+b)∈ΔN−1,x∈ℝd.f(x)=\mathrm{softmax}(Wx+b)\in\Delta^{N-1},\qquad x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.

Here ΔN−1:={p∈ℝN:pi≥0,∀i,∑i=1Npi=1}\Delta^{N-1}:=\{p\in\mathbb{R}^{N}:\ p_{i}\geq 0,\ \forall i,\ \sum_{i=1}^{N}p_{i}=1\} denotes the probability simplex. Let wi⊤w_{i}^{\top} denote the ii-th row of WW and define

supx∈ℝd‖∇f​(x)‖2→1=12​D​(W),\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}\|\nabla f(x)\|_{2\to 1}=\frac{1}{2}\,D(W),

Proof.

For z∈ℝNz\in\mathbb{R}^{N}, write p=softmax⁡(z)∈ΔN−1p=\mathrm{softmax}(z)\in\Delta^{N-1} and recall

J⁡(p)=∇zsoftmax​(z)=Diag⁡(p)−p​p⊤.J(p)=\nabla_{z}\,\mathrm{softmax}(z)=\mathrm{Diag}(p)-pp^{\top}.

By the chain rule, for p=softmax⁡(W​x+b)p=\mathrm{softmax}(Wx+b) we have

∇f​(x)=J​(p)​W.\nabla f(x)=J(p)\,W.

Hence

supx∈ℝd‖∇f​(x)‖2→1=supp∈ΔN−1‖J⁡(p)​W‖2→1.\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}\|\nabla f(x)\|_{2\to 1}=\sup_{p\in\Delta^{N-1}}\|J(p)W\|_{2\to 1}. (19)

Fix p∈ΔN−1p\in\Delta^{N-1} and v∈ℝNv\in\mathbb{R}^{N}. Let μ:=p⊤​v\mu:=p^{\top}v. Using

J⁡(p)​v=(Diag⁡(p)−p​p⊤)​v=Diag⁡(p)​(v−μ​𝟏),J(p)v=(\mathrm{Diag}(p)-pp^{\top})v=\mathrm{Diag}(p)\bigl(v-\mu\mathbf{1}\bigr),

supp∈ΔN−1∑i=1Npi​|vi−p⊤​v|=r2.\sup_{p\in\Delta^{N-1}}\sum_{i=1}^{N}p_{i}\,|v_{i}-p^{\top}v|=\frac{r}{2}. (21)

∑i=1Npi​|vi−μ|≤(∑i=1Npi)1/2​(∑i=1Npi​(vi−μ)2)1/2=Varp​(v).\sum_{i=1}^{N}p_{i}|v_{i}-\mu|\leq\Big(\sum_{i=1}^{N}p_{i}\Big)^{1/2}\Big(\sum_{i=1}^{N}p_{i}(v_{i}-\mu)^{2}\Big)^{1/2}=\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}_{p}(v)}.

p=12​(eimax+eimin).p=\frac{1}{2}(e_{i_{\max}}+e_{i_{\min}}).

Combining (20) and (21), for any u∈ℝdu\in\mathbb{R}^{d} with ‖u‖2=1\|u\|_{2}=1,

supp∈ΔN−1‖J⁡(p)​W​u‖1=12​(maxi⁡(W​u)i−minj⁡(W​u)j).\sup_{p\in\Delta^{N-1}}\|J(p)Wu\|_{1}=\frac{1}{2}\Big(\max_{i}(Wu)_{i}-\min_{j}(Wu)_{j}\Big). (22)

maxi⁡(W​u)i−minj⁡(W​u)j=maxi,j⁡(wi−wj)⊤​u.\max_{i}(Wu)_{i}-\min_{j}(Wu)_{j}=\max_{i,j}(w_{i}-w_{j})^{\top}u.

supx∈ℝd‖∇f​(x)‖2→1\displaystyle\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}\|\nabla f(x)\|_{2\to 1}

=\displaystyle= sup‖u‖2=1supp∈ΔN−1‖J⁡(p)​W​u‖1\displaystyle\sup_{\|u\|_{2}=1}\sup_{p\in\Delta^{N-1}}\|J(p)Wu\|_{1}
=\displaystyle= 12​sup‖u‖2=1(maxi⁡(W​u)i−minj⁡(W​u)j)\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\sup_{\|u\|_{2}=1}\Big(\max_{i}(Wu)_{i}-\min_{j}(Wu)_{j}\Big)
=\displaystyle= 12​D​(W).\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\,D(W).

Based on the previous theory for the Lipschitz constant of MLPs by Fazlyab et al. (2020), we obtain the following direct result:

Appendix E Additional Experiments

E.1 Experiments on Estimator Sensitivity

In this section, we conduct a sensitivity analysis of the proposed estimators S^C​o​v\hat{S}_{Cov} and S^C​p​t\hat{S}_{Cpt} with respect to the parameter β\beta. We take the ”-90%” domain of ColoredMNIST as the target domain and regard the mixture of the other two domains as the source domain. We train the model on the source domain using ERM with the best hyperparameters in DomainBed. At the last checkpoint, we store all representation-label pairs from both the source and target domains. For each β\beta, we randomly sample 10,000 pairs from each domain, run the DataShifts algorithm to obtain the estimated results, repeat this procedure 50 times, and report the average. The results are shown below:

Across magnitude changes in β\beta, the coefficients of variation of S^C​o​v\hat{S}_{Cov} and S^C​p​t\hat{S}_{Cpt} are 1.076% and 0.990%, so both estimators are stable for small β\beta. Since entropic OT gets faster as β\beta grows, we use β=0.2\beta=0.2 in the main experiments to balance speed and accuracy.

E.2 Experiments on the Bias under Stochastic Labeling

We test the bias of our γ∗\gamma^{*}-Y∣\midX shift estimator S^C​p​t\hat{S}_{Cpt} on the following stochastic-labeling synthetic data. In both source and target domains, covariates are drawn from a 10-dim standard normal distributions. At each xx, scalar labels are sampled from normal distribution 𝒩⁡(‖x‖2,σ2)\mathcal{N}(\|x\|_{2},\sigma^{2}) in the source and 𝒩⁡(‖x‖2+1.0,σ2)\mathcal{N}(\|x\|_{2}+1.0,\sigma^{2}) in the target. Thus, the true Y∣\midX shift SC​p​tγ∗=1.0S_{Cpt}^{\gamma^{*}}=1.0, and standard deviation σ\sigma controls the noise. By Proposition 4.7, the irreducible errors of both domains are σ2\sigma^{2}, and the bias Δ≥0\Delta\geq 0 of our estimator should be bounded by 2​σ2\sigma. Δ^=S^C​p​t−SC​p​tγ∗\hat{\Delta}=\hat{S}_{Cpt}-S_{Cpt}^{\gamma^{*}} is an estimate of the bias Δ\Delta. For each σ\sigma, we randomly sample 10,000 points from each domain, and run DataShifts algorithm with β=0.2\beta=0.2, repeat this procedure 50 times, and report the average Δ^\hat{\Delta}. The results are shown below:

When the noise σ\sigma is small, the bias Δ^\hat{\Delta} is also very small, which means our estimator S^C​p​t\hat{S}_{Cpt} stays close to the true Y∣\midX shift SC​p​tγ∗=1.0S_{Cpt}^{\gamma^{*}}=1.0. Even when the noise in both domains reaches half of the true Y∣\midX shift (σ=0.5\sigma=0.5), the bias Δ^\hat{\Delta} remains small, and the S^C​p​t\hat{S}_{Cpt} still does not notably overestimate. As σ\sigma grows far beyond 1.0, Y∣\midX shift becomes less identifiable. The bias increases and overestimation appears, but it stays below the bound set by irreducible error, as proved in Proposition 4.7.
